## 1. Courts: legality / procedure / constitutionality
- **Statutory authority:** Trump used **INA §212(f)** (“suspension of entry of aliens” for national interest). That section has been upheld before (e.g. *Trump v. Hawaii*, the travel ban case). It gives a president broad power to block classes of entrants.  
- **Problem here:** this isn’t just a travel restriction, it’s a **massive new fee**. Normally, visa fees are set by **USCIS rulemaking under APA** (Administrative Procedure Act), with public comment. Using 212(f) to impose a $100k surcharge looks like an **end run around Congress’s power of the purse**.  
- **Likely arguments in court:**  
  - *Ultra vires* (beyond statutory authority).  
  - *APA violation* (no notice-and-comment).  
  - *Equal protection / due process* if applied discriminatorily.  
- **Precedent:** SCOTUS gave wide latitude before, but attaching a dollar figure (especially revenue-generating) may shift the balance. That’s where challengers will hammer.  
- **Expectation:** TRO/PI (temporary restraining order / preliminary injunction) hearings within **weeks**. Courts may enjoin *parts* of the order (the fee) while leaving a narrower security-based entry restriction intact.

Zohran Kwame Mamdani[c] (born October 18, 1991) is an American politician who has served since 2021 as a member of the New York State Assembly from the 36th district, based in Queens. A member of the Democratic Party and the Democratic Socialists of America, he is the Democratic nominee for mayor of New York City in the 2025 election.

Mamdani was born in Kampala, Uganda, into an Indian family, to academic Mahmood Mamdani and filmmaker Mira Nair. The family immigrated to South Africa when he was five years old and then to the United States when he was seven, settling in New York City. Mamdani graduated from the Bronx High School of Science and earned a bachelor's degree in Africana studies from Bowdoin College.

After working as a housing counselor and hip-hop musician, he entered local politics as a campaign manager for Khader El-Yateem and Ross Barkan. Mamdani was first elected to the New York State Assembly in 2020, defeating four-term incumbent Aravella Simotas in the Democratic primary. He was reelected without opposition in 2022 and 2024.

In October 2024, Mamdani announced his candidacy for mayor of New York City in the 2025 election. His campaign platform includes support for fare-free city buses; public child care; city-owned grocery stores; a rent freeze on rent-stabilized units; additional affordable housing units; comprehensive public safety reform; and a $30 minimum wage by 2030. Mamdani also supports tax increases on corporations and those earning above $1 million annually.

He has been sharply critical of Israel's treatment of Palestinians, pledging to abide by the International Criminal Court arrest warrants for Israeli leaders by arresting Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu if he visits New York City. During the Democratic primaries, Mamdani was endorsed by prominent progressive politicians, including Bernie Sanders, Ilhan Omar, and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. On June 24, 2025, Mamdani defeated former governor Andrew Cuomo and nine other candidates to become the Democratic nominee.

Early life and education
Mamdani was born on October 18, 1991, in Kampala, Uganda, the only child of filmmaker Mira Nair and postcolonialism academic Mahmood Mamdani.[11][12] He was given his middle name, Kwame, by his father in honor of Kwame Nkrumah, the first President of Ghana.[13][14] Both his parents are of Indian descent; his mother is a Punjabi Hindu[15][16][17] who was born in Rourkela and raised in Bhubaneswar,[18] and his father is a Gujarati Muslim who was born in Bombay and grew up primarily in Uganda.[19] His paternal grandparents were born in present-day Tanzania and his father's family was part of the Indian diaspora in Southeast Africa.[19] His maternal grandmother was a social worker and founder of the Salaam Baalak Trust.[20]

Mamdani lived in Kampala until he was five, when his family moved to Cape Town, in South Africa's Western Cape province.[11] He attended St. George's Grammar School in Mowbray while his father taught African studies at the University of Cape Town.[14] The family then moved to America, settling in New York City when Mamdani was seven, and he was raised in Morningside Heights.[21] He has described his upbringing as "privileged", saying, "I never had to want for something, and yet I knew that was not in any way the reality for most New Yorkers."[22]

Mamdani attended the Bank Street School for Children on the Upper West Side of Manhattan, where he successfully ran as the independent candidate in a middle school mock election, adopting a platform of "equal rights, anti-war [policy] that proposed spending money on education rather than the military".[23] In 2003, he returned to Kampala for a year and attended school during his father's sabbatical there;[19] his paternal grandparents and aunt still live there and helped take care of him while his father was working on the book Good Muslim, Bad Muslim.[24]

Mamdani graduated from the Bronx High School of Science in Kingsbridge Heights,[25] where he co-founded the school's first cricket team[12] and unsuccessfully ran for student body vice president.[26] He also played soccer with the West Side Soccer League.[27] Mamdani then attended Bowdoin College in Brunswick, Maine, where he co-founded the school's chapter of Students for Justice in Palestine. He graduated in 2014 with a bachelor's degree in Africana studies.[28][29]

Career
Before running for office, Mamdani worked as a foreclosure prevention and housing counselor. There, he assisted lower-income non-white homeowners in Queens with eviction notices and efforts to remain in their homes.[30] He said the experience motivated him to run for office to address the housing and affordability crisis.[30]

Music career
Mamdani is a fan of hip-hop and has composed and produced rap music.[31] In 2016, under the moniker Young Cardamom, he collaborated with Ugandan rapper HAB on an EP titled Sidda Mukyaalo, which is Luganda for "No going back to the village".[32] The duo performed at that year's Nyege Nyege festival in Jinja, Uganda.[33] They first started working together in 2015, and their first song was Kanda [Chap Chap], about chapati, an Indian food that has been adopted as a Ugandan staple. Both rap in English and Luganda (and HAB also raps in Nubi and Swahili), and Mamdani said the "lyrics and choice of language are rebuttals of what Ugandan society expects of us—that someone with some South Sudanese roots is forever 'Nubi' and that Indian Ugandans are actually just Indians in Uganda".[34] Mamdani also credits Ugandan producer Hannz Tactiq, who provided the beat and would "record, mix & master" for them, and in whose studio they worked until late at night.[33][34] In 2019, Mamdani released a single titled "Nani" under the moniker Mr. Cardamom, an homage to his maternal grandmother,[35] whom he described as "a source of joy, wisdom, and love".[36] Cookbook author and actress Madhur Jaffrey is featured in the single's music video, playing his grandmother.[37]

Mamdani curated and produced the soundtrack for his mother Mira Nair's 2016 film Queen of Katwe.[38][39] As the film's music supervisor, he was nominated in the 2017 Guild of Music Supervisors Awards.[40]

Early political involvement
Mamdani entered New York City politics as a volunteer for Ali Najmi's campaign in the 2015 special election for the 23rd district of the City Council.[13][31] In 2017, Mamdani joined the New York City chapter of Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) and worked for the campaign of New York City Council candidate Khader El-Yateem, a Palestinian Lutheran minister and democratic socialist from Bay Ridge, Brooklyn.[13] Mamdani served as the campaign manager for Ross Barkan's 2018 bid for the New York State Senate and was also a field organizer for fellow democratic socialist Tiffany Cabán's 2019 campaign for Queens County District Attorney.[13][41]

New York State Assembly (2020–present)

Mamdani at the Resist Fascism Rally in Bryant Park (October 27, 2024)
In October 2019, Mamdani announced his campaign to represent New York's 36th State Assembly district, which encompasses Astoria and Long Island City in Queens.[42][43] He was endorsed by the DSA,[44] running on a platform of housing reform, police and prison reform, and public ownership of utilities.[42] Mamdani's June 2020 primary victory over four-term Democratic incumbent Aravella Simotas took almost a month to call,[45] and he won the general election with no Republican opposition in November.[46] Mamdani was reelected without opposition in 2022[47] and 2024.[48]

Mamdani is a member of the DSA's nine-member "State Socialists in Office" bloc in New York and a member of the Muslim Democratic Club of New York.[13][49][50] Mamdani was the keynote speaker at the 2023 DSA convention, saying, "We are special as DSA electeds not because of ourselves; we are special because of our organization".[51][52]

As of January 2025, Mamdani was a member of nine Assembly committees: the Committee on Aging; the Committee on Cities; the Committee on Election Law; the Committee on Energy; the Committee on Real Property Taxation; the Black, Puerto Rican, Hispanic & Asian Legislative Caucus; the Puerto Rican/Hispanic Task Force; the Asian Pacific American Task Force; and the Task Force on New Americans.[53]

Mamdani had been the primary sponsor of 20 bills in the Assembly—three of which became law—and the co-sponsor of 238 bills as of May 2025.[54] As of March 2025, he was the only state legislator in the mayoral race not to miss a session in Albany in 2025.[55]

As a member of the Assembly, Mamdani helped to launch a successful fare-free bus pilot program and participated in a hunger strike alongside taxi drivers.[55][56]

2025 New York City mayoral campaign
Main articles: 2025 New York City Democratic mayoral primary and 2025 New York City mayoral election

Mamdani mayoral campaign logo
On October 23, 2024, Mamdani announced his candidacy for mayor of New York City in 2025.[57] His platform includes support for free city buses and a rent freeze in rent-stabilized housing.[58][59][60] Mamdani also wants the city government to operate five grocery stores—one in each borough—to drive down grocery prices.[61] Mamdani's platform includes support for universal child care and for the construction of 200,000 new affordable housing units.[62] He also supports public safety reform and a $30 minimum wage by 2030.[63] His platform calls for tax increases on corporations and those earning above $1 million annually.[64] He has been critical of the state of Israel's treatment of the Palestinian people, pledging to abide by an International Criminal Court warrant by arresting Benjamin Netanyahu if he were to visit New York City.[65][66]


Volunteers for Mamdani
For most of the campaign, Mamdani trailed Cuomo in polling. While he and Cuomo raised similar amounts of money, his donor base was considerably larger than Cuomo's.[67] A poll taken shortly before the June 24 primary election showed that Mamdani had caught up to Cuomo.[68] First-choice results on election night showed Mamdani had a large lead over Cuomo,[69][70] who conceded the race that evening.[71] On July 1, after the New York City Board of Elections released its ranked-choice ballot tabulation, the Associated Press announced Mamdani had won the Democratic primary.[72] It was considered a major upset.[73]

On August 23, the Mamdani campaign released a video teaser[74] for an August 24 "Zcavenger" scavenger hunt across New York, an opportunity to test people's familiarity with the city's political history and knowledge of bus and subway routes. The campaign had 500 printed participant cards, but more people turned out to participate.[75][76][77][78]

Political positions

Mamdani identifies as a democratic socialist.[41] He is a member of the Democratic Socialists of America.[50][61] Mamdani has also been described as a progressive.[79]

Influences
Mamdani has credited his parents for both fostering his interest in politics and world affairs and shaping his outlook on them. He has noted that, when he was growing up, his household frequently discussed these subjects.[80] He has credited Bernie Sanders's 2016 presidential campaign for inspiring him to become a democratic socialist.[41] Mamdani is also influenced by 20th-century American "sewer socialists" such as Milwaukee Mayor Daniel Hoan and Congressman Victor L. Berger, as well as the populist New York City mayor Fiorello La Guardia.[81]

During his mayoral campaign, Mamdani has cited Boston mayor Michelle Wu and Baltimore mayor Brandon Scott as two mayors whose leadership he will seek to emulate if elected.[82] He has frequently pointed to Wu, whom he has called the most effective current Democratic politician in the U.S.,[83] as a role model for both her performance as mayor and prior work as a city councilor.[84][85] Wu is a progressive but, unlike Mamdani, does not identify as a socialist.[85]

Childcare and education
Mamdani supports a universal pre-kindergarten childcare system.[86][87][88] He has proposed giving all new New York City families "baby baskets" containing products such as diapers and nursing supplies.[89] Mamdani introduced a bill to eliminate New York University's and Columbia University's state property tax exemption and direct those funds to the City University of New York system, which has historically struggled with funding.[90]

Protection of Hasidic yeshivas
In an interview with Der Blatt, a newspaper associated with the Hasidic movement of Judaism, Mamdani expressed a desire to defend Hasidic yeshivas (institutions for Torah study) from accusations of failing to meet state educational standards.[91] He stated that "I will listen to your leaders" on education and "I will work to protect you from anyone who wants to disturb your way of life".[91]

Crime and policing
Mamdani has argued that increasing policing and incarceration does little to prevent harm and that "dignified work, economic stability, and well-resourced neighborhoods" can more effectively keep the public safe.[92] He has advocated a more community-based approach to reducing crime, focusing on homeless outreach and anti-violence programs. He contends that there is too much reliance on police to fix societal problems, saying, "Police have a critical role to play, but right now we are relying on them to deal with the failures of the social safety net of reliance that is preventing them from doing their actual jobs."[93] He has proposed a Department of Community Safety to expand mental health outreach.[61] This proposed civilian-led department would deploy mental health teams to respond to 911 calls and expand street-level programs intended to stop the cycle of violence, as well as focusing on programs "that are proven to create long-term stability and promote recovery."[94]

In a June 2020 tweet, Mamdani wrote, "We don't need an investigation to know that the NYPD is racist, anti-queer & a major threat to public safety. What we need is to #DefundTheNYPD."[95][96] During the 2025 mayoral race, he said he would work with the police rather than defund them, emphasizing their importance in dealing with violent crime and the role of social workers and mental health professionals in addressing underlying causes and prevention.[97] In September 2025, Mamdani said he would apologize for describing the NYPD as racist.[98]

In September 2025, Mamdani condemned the murder of Charlie Kirk, saying that political violence has no place in the United States.[99]

Economic policy
Mamdani advocates for debt relief among taxi medallion owners.[100]

Mamdani has advocated rent control, strengthening tenant protections, and creating a Social Housing Development Agency that would build publicly owned affordable housing.[101] He wants to build 200,000 new units of affordable, rent-stabilized homes over the next 10 years and double the amount of spending to rehabilitate homes for the city's 400,000 public housing tenants.[102] He also wants to "increase density around mass transit hubs" and "upzone wealthier neighborhoods", citing housing policies in Jersey City and Tokyo as examples.[103]

Mamdani supports raising New York City's minimum wage to $30 per hour by 2030.[104] He advocates a pilot program in which the city government would operate one grocery store in each borough to drive down prices.[61][105]

Mamdani supports an increase in corporate taxes in New York State from 7.25% to 11.5%, to match those of New Jersey.[106] He also supports a new 2% increase for income tax on city residents who earn more than $1 million a year,[102] to raise $20 billion to fund tuition-free CUNY and SUNY schools, statewide universal childcare, a subway fare freeze, free MTA buses, and tenant protections.[107] In June 2025, Mamdani said, "I don't think we should have billionaires."[108]

Mamdani made a mayoral campaign pledge to reduce taxes on "overtaxed homeowners in the outer boroughs" of New York City, while advocating to increase taxes on "more expensive homes in richer and whiter neighborhoods."[109][110] His intention with this policy was to tackle a 1981 property tax law that essentially taxes owners of expensive homes based on the homes' potential rental price rather than their market value, which could lead to the owners paying much less property tax than owners of cheap homes.[111]

Environment
Mamdani views climate action as essential to achieving social justice in New York City. In 2021, he organized volunteers and lobbied Governor Kathy Hochul to prevent the expansion of a gas-fired peaker power plant in Astoria, citing environmental concerns for low-income nonwhite communities.[112][113] Mamdani has also backed statewide measures such as the All-Electric Buildings Act, which prohibits installing fossil-fuel equipment (e.g., gas stoves) in new buildings, and supported introducing congestion pricing in Manhattan to reduce traffic-related emissions.[114][115]

As a mayoral candidate, Mamdani proposed a comprehensive decarbonization and resilience agenda. His "Green Schools for a Healthier New York City" blueprint would retrofit 500 public school buildings with rooftop solar arrays and upgraded HVAC systems; build 500 green schoolyards; transform heat-absorbing asphalt into green space serving students and community residents; convert 50 schools into year-round resilience hubs to offer shelter and resources during extreme heat, storms, or flooding; and extend tax incentives such as J-51 benefits to support building owners' compliance with Local Law 97.[114][116]

Healthcare
Mamdani supports the New York Health Act, which would establish single-payer healthcare in New York State.[117] He portrayed a firefighter in a 2021 advertisement for the Campaign for New York Health.[117]

Foreign policy
Israeli–Palestinian conflict
Mamdani is deeply critical of Israel, condemning Israeli apartheid in 2023.[118] He supports the Boycott, Divestment, and Sanctions movement,[119] and in 2023 introduced a state assembly bill to prohibit registered charities from donating to organizations involved in Israel's illegal West Bank settlements; a later iteration of the bill added organizations lending support to alleged war crimes in Gaza.[120][50]

The day after the Hamas-led October 7 attacks on Israel, Mamdani issued a statement to "mourn the hundreds of people killed across Israel and Palestine" and saying that the end of "occupation" and "apartheid" was the only path to peace.[121][118][122] He later condemned the Hamas attacks as a "horrific war crime".[118][123] The next week, Mamdani was arrested during a pro-Palestinian ceasefire demonstration.[124][125][126][123] In 2025, Mamdani said he believed Israel was committing genocide in Gaza,[127][119] and that if Benjamin Netanyahu travels to New York City, he should be arrested in accordance with the International Criminal Court's warrant for his arrest.[128][129]

Iran–Israel war
Mamdani condemned US airstrikes on Iranian nuclear sites during the Iran–Israel war, describing them as unconstitutional and destabilizing.[130]

India
Mamdani has said he would refuse to appear with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi if Modi visited New York, as he considers Modi a "war criminal", accusing him of "orchestrat[ing] a mass slaughter of Muslims in Gujarat" during 2002 riots in which 790 Muslims and 254 Hindus died.[131] He compared Modi to Israel's Netanyahu.[132] Mamdani said that in the aftermath of these events, few Muslims remain in Gujarat, and that most people believe Gujarati Muslims do not exist today, a claim Indian leaders disputed.[133]

Social issues
Mamdani supported Proposal 1, a 2024 amendment to the Constitution of New York that made it unconstitutional to engage in discrimination based on ethnicity, national origin, age, disability, sex (including sexual orientation, gender identity, and gender expression), pregnancy and pregnancy-related outcomes, and reproductive healthcare and autonomy.[134][135][136]

Immigration
Mamdani supports enforcement of New York's sanctuary laws, which bar Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) from entering schools, hospitals, and city property without a judicial warrant, and has advocated for stronger sanctuary laws.[137] He has also proposed creating a commission to ensure compliance by city agencies and contractors.[138] He has pledged that if he is elected mayor, the city will provide legal representation for all immigrants in detention proceedings.[139]

On March 12, 2025, Mamdani confronted former United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) acting director Tom Homan in Albany about ICE's recent arrest of student activist Mahmoud Khalil. Mamdani yelled, "Do you believe in the First Amendment?"[140]

LGBTQ+ rights
Mamdani supports LGBTQ+ rights.[141][142] He aims to establish NYC as an LGBTQ+ sanctuary city and establish the Office of LGBTQIA+ Affairs to "expand and centralize the services, programs, and support that LGBTQIA+ New Yorkers need across housing, employment, and more."[143][144] Mamdani says LGBTQ+ people who became homeless due to their identity would benefit from his cost-of-living policies.[142]

Mamdani appeared at a February 2025 rally in Union Square to protest an executive order signed by President Trump that threatened to "withhold federal funding from hospitals that provide gender-affirming treatments to trans youth".[145][146] As part of his platform, he supports expanding and protecting gender-affirming care citywide. He proposed an immediate investment of $65 million in public providers to ensure funding for medical treatments that lose Medicaid coverage and promised to ensure hospital accountability.[144]

Transportation
Mamdani supports permanently eliminating bus fares.[147][148][149] He advocated for a fare-free pilot program on MTA buses,[150][151] which was launched on the Q4, B60, Bx18, M116 and S46/96 routes in September 2023.[152][153] The program saw a 30% increase in ridership on weekdays, predominantly from people earning less than $28,000 a year. Across the five routes made free, assaults on bus operators dropped by 38.9%.[154] The fare-free program ended in August 2024 after state lawmakers did not reauthorize it.[155][156] In response, Mamdani said, "the MTA was opposed to this program ... because they were saying that now is not the time to create any kind of confusion around fare collection."[150][157] He estimates that it would cost New York City $650 million per year to eliminate bus fares.[158]

In December 2022, Mamdani introduced a series of bills for the 2023 session called "Fix the MTA". He proposed free bus travel over the next four years across the Bronx, Brooklyn, Queens, and then Manhattan and Staten Island.[159] The Formula Three Act would fill the $2.5 billion shortfall of the MTA with another plank freezing fares at $2.75. Another plank would have set aside further money for more frequency, such as six-minute headways for trains and the 100 most-used bus routes, then using any additional funds to increase service by 20%.[160]

In 2023, Mamdani co-introduced a bill to enact a weight-based vehicle-registration fee to dissuade people from owning heavier vehicles in an effort to make streets safer.[161] Mamdani supports congestion pricing in New York City and drafted a bill with New York state senator Michael Gianaris titled "Get Congestion Pricing Right" to increase bus service frequency and increase the number of fare-free buses.[162]

Personal life
Mamdani is a dual citizen of Uganda and the United States; he was naturalized in the latter country in 2018.[1] He is Shia Muslim and identifies with the Twelver branch.[28][163] In February 2025, Mamdani married Syrian-American animator, Rama Duwaji in a civil ceremony at New York City Hall.[164] The couple met years earlier on the dating application Hinge, and held a private nikah ceremony in December 2024.[165] Mamdani and Duwaji reside in Astoria, Queens.[13]

Mamdani is a fan of the New York Mets and the New York Giants.[166] He also supports the English football club Arsenal.[167] Besides English, Mamdani has spoken other languages during his mayoral campaign, showing different degrees of proficiency in Hindi–Urdu, Bengali, and Spanish.[168][169][170]

### Key Mamdani Life Events (with timestamps we can anchor)
- **Birth:** Oct 18, 1991 – Kampala, Uganda.  
- **Migration:** ~1996 (family moved to South Africa, he was 5).  
- **Migration to U.S.:** ~1998 (family moved to NYC, he was 7).  
- **Schooling:** Bronx High School of Science (late 2000s), Bowdoin College graduation 2014.  
- **Music career:** First collab ~2015; Nyege Nyege Festival performance 2016.  
- **Naturalization:** Became U.S. citizen 2018.  
- **Political debut:** Campaign manager 2017–2018; ran for Assembly 2019; elected Nov 2020; sworn Jan 1, 2021.  
- **Reelections:** 2022, 2024.  
- **Mayoral candidacy:** Announced Oct 23, 2024.  
- **Marriage:** Civil ceremony NYC Feb 2025, nikah Dec 2024.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
2015 Russian Sukhoi Su-24 shootdown

The Su-24M aircraft that was shot down, two weeks before the event.
Incident
Date	24 November 2015
Summary	Shot down by Turkish F-16 fighter jet
Site	Syria–Turkey border
Aircraft
Aircraft type	Sukhoi Su-24M
Operator	 Russian Air Force
Registration	RF-90932 / 83 White
Flight origin	Khmeimim Air Base, Syria
Occupants	2
Crew	2
Fatalities	1
Survivors	1
vte
Syrian–Turkish border clashes during the Syrian Civil War
vte
Syrian War spillover and international incidents
On 24 November 2015, a Turkish Air Force F-16 fighter jet shot down a Russian Sukhoi Su-24M attack aircraft near the Syria–Turkey border.[1][2] According to Turkey, the aircraft was fired upon while in Turkish airspace because it violated the border up to a depth of 2.19 kilometres (1.36 miles) for about 17 seconds after being warned to change its heading ten times over a period of five minutes before entering the airspace.[3][4] The Russia Defence Ministry denied that the aircraft ever left Syrian airspace, claiming that their satellite data showed that the Sukhoi was about 1,000 metres (1,100 yd) inside Syrian airspace when it was shot down.[5]

The U.S. State Department said that the U.S. independently confirmed that the aircraft's flight path violated Turkish territory, and that the Turks gave multiple warnings to the pilot, to which they received no response and released audio recordings of the warnings they had broadcast.[6][7] Turkish president Recep Tayyip Erdoğan pointed out that Turkey had the right to defend its airspace.[8] Although Russian president Vladimir Putin said that the U.S. knew the flight path of the Russian jet and should have informed Turkey, two U.S. officials said that Russia had not informed the U.S. military of its jet's flight plan.[9]

The Russian pilot and navigator both ejected from the aircraft. The navigator Konstantin Murakhtin was rescued, but the pilot Oleg Peshkov was shot and killed by Syrian rebel ground fire while descending by parachute.[10] A Russian marine from the search and rescue team launched to retrieve the two airmen was also killed when a rescue helicopter was targeted by the rebels.[10][11]

The incident was the first destruction of a Russian or Soviet Air Forces warplane by a NATO member state since an attack on the Sui-ho Dam during the Korean War in 1953.[12][13][14] Reactions to the incident included denunciation from Russia and an attempt to defuse the situation by NATO afterwards. Russia deployed the guided missile cruiser Moskva armed with S-300F (SA-N-6 Grumble) long-range SAM missiles off the Syrian coast near Latakia[15] and S-400 (SA-21 Growler) mobile SAM systems to Khmeimim airbase. In response, the Turkish Armed Forces deployed the KORAL land-based radar electronic support system in Hatay Province along the Turkish–Syrian border.[16][17]

Background
Further information: Turkish involvement in the Syrian Civil War, Russian military intervention in the Syrian Civil War, and Spillover of the Syrian Civil War

Turkish President Erdoğan (left) and Russian President Putin at the G-20 summit in Antalya on 15 November 2015
After the 2012 shooting down of a Turkish RF-4E Phantom II Jet by Syrian forces, Turkish prime minister Recep Tayyip Erdoğan protested, saying that brief incursions should not trigger an attack, pointing out that Turkey did not shoot down Syrian helicopters that strayed into Turkish airspace.[18][19][20] Nevertheless, as a response to the event he announced that Turkey changed its rules of engagement, and said it would start to consider all "military elements" approaching from Syria an enemy threat and would act accordingly.[21][22] Subsequently, Turkey shot down a Syrian Mi-17 helicopter in September 2013[23] and a MiG-23 warplane in March 2014.[24]

Russia is one of several countries directly involved in the Syrian conflict. On 30 September 2015, Russia began its air campaign in support of the SAA against Syrian rebels.

In early October, Turkey and NATO protested against what they saw as Russia's deliberate violations of Turkish airspace.[25][a] The Russian defence ministry admitted that a Russian Su-30 aircraft had entered Turkish airspace "for a few seconds" because of bad weather, adding that measures had been taken to prevent a repeat of such incidents, however Turkish radar had tracked the aircraft straying into Turkish airspace for up to 8 km (5 mi) lasting "several minutes".[32][33][34] From 3–15 October, five discussions between senior ranking officials from Turkey and Russia occurred, concerning Turkish rules of engagement and Russian violations of Turkish airspace.[35][36][37][38] On 6 November 2015, six U.S. Air Force F-15C fighters were deployed by US European Command from the 48th Fighter Wing at their Lakenheath base in Britain to Incirlik Air Base as part of Operation Inherent Resolve.[22][39] The government of Turkey requested these to secure the sovereignty of Turkish airspace because of earlier repeated Russian intrusions into Turkish airspace.[22][39]

On 19 November, Russian ambassador to Turkey Andrei Karlov and the Russian military attaché, Colonel Andrei Victorovich Dovger, were summoned by Turkey.[40] Russia, which was criticised by Turkey for having conducted operations near the Turkish border, a region inhabited by Syrian Turkmen and largely free of ISIL (though al-Nusra Front, the al-Qaeda affiliate in Syria, was present in the region),[41][42] was notified that Turkey's rules of engagement were in place and it would react to any violations of its border security. Turkey also warned Russia that it would not be indifferent to "attacks targeting the life security of Turkmen" in the Bayırbucak area.[43][44] The preceding week Turkey had called for the UN Security Council to discuss attacks against Turkish-backed Turkmens.[45] Approximately 1,700 people had fled the area in the previous three days due to battles between Syrian government forces and anti-government Syrian Turkmen and al-Nusra Front fighters.[42] Russia had bombed the area near the Turkish border to support Syrian government forces.[45] Syrian Turkmen formed their own armed brigades called Syrian Turkmen Brigades in opposition to the Syrian government of President Bashar al-Assad, loosely affiliated with other rebels such as the Free Syrian Army. The Turkmen brigades also cooperated with al-Qaeda's Syrian affiliate the al-Nusra Front and with the Salafi coalition known as Ahrar al-Sham.[46] In Latakia, the Turkish-supported rebels formed the Jabal al-Turkman Brigade.[46]

The shootdown

Approximate flight paths according to the Turkish and Russian forces.
On 24 November 2015 at 9:24 am local time (7:24 am GMT),[8] as it was returning to Khmeimim airbase, a Russian Sukhoi Su-24 aircraft with tail number 83 white and registration number RF-90932[47] was shot down near the Syrian–Turkish border by a missile from a patrolling Turkish Air Force F-16 fighter jet.[48][49] Later analysis suggested that a radar-guided, medium range AIM-120 AMRAAM was fired from between 14–19 kilometres (9–12 mi) away.[50] The Economist reported that the two Su-24s were on their way to strike Syrian Turkmen targets.[44] Syrian government forces supported by the Shiite militias and the Russian Air Force were fighting against Syrian Turkmen brigades, Army of Conquest and al-Nusra Front fighters.[42]

Early reports from Russian news agencies citing the Russian Defence Ministry, indicated that the aircraft had been downed by a ground-based strike from Syrian Turkmen rebels, but they later confirmed Turkish reports that the aircraft had been shot down by Turkish fighter jets.[citation needed] The Turkish military released a graphic of the Russian aircraft's flight pattern, which shows it crossing the southern tip of Hatay Province before being shot down and crashing near Turkmen Mountain.[51][52] Russia then countered Turkey's radar trace analysis by publishing a different flight map showing no airspace violation.[53][54] Three days later, on 27 November, Russia published another map.[55]

According to Turkey's statement to the UN Security Council, two aircraft, whose nationalities were unknown at the time, violated Turkish airspace up to a depth of 2.19 km (1.36 mi) for about 17 seconds.[3][56] According to Turkish officials, the aircraft were given 10 warnings within the span of 5 minutes, by operators at a ground-controlled interception station, to change their course.[51] Turkey later released the audio recording ("The unknown air traffic position to Humaymim 020 radial 26 miles. This is Turkish Air Force speaking on Guard. You are approaching Turkish airspace, change your heading south immediately").[57][58][59] The Russians claim there were no warnings.[60] Analysts have noted that Turkey's warnings were issued on a dedicated mutually-agreed radio channel, which was the international Guard (emergency) channel (243.0 MHz), but the R-862M radio fitted to the Su-24M is not able to monitor this channel without optional equipment, which may not have been installed.[61][62] According to Turkey, one aircraft left Turkish national airspace after violating it; the other aircraft was fired upon by Turkish F-16s patrolling the area and crashed into Syrian territory after being hit in Turkish airspace.[3] Based on its heat signature, an anonymous American official stated that the jet was hit in Syrian airspace after a short incursion into Turkey.[63] On 30 November, US Ambassador to NATO Douglas Lute stated that the data supported the Turkish version of events.[64]

According to the Russian Defence Ministry, the Su-24 was downed from an altitude of 6,000 metres (20,000 ft) within one kilometre of the Turkish border and in Syrian airspace, while returning to the Khmeimim airbase in Syria.[49] Russia has maintained that the aircraft never left Syrian territory.[48] The Russian Defence Ministry confirmed the aircraft was an Su-24 but said that it had proof the jet was within Syrian airspace.[51] According to the commander-in-chief of the Russian Aerospace Forces, Viktor Bondarev, a Turkish F-16 entered Syria's airspace for 40 seconds and flew 2 km (1.2 mi) inside Syrian territory, but the Russian warplane did not violate the Turkish border.[65]

Casualties

Repatriation of Oleg Peshkov's body at Chkalovsky Airport, 30 November 2015.
Both pilots ejected after the aircraft was hit.[51] Initially, the deputy commander of a Turkmen Syrian opposition rebel brigade in Syria, Alparslan Çelik (a Turkish citizen and member of the Grey Wolves ultra-nationalist group[66][67]), claimed his forces had shot dead the two pilots as they descended with parachutes,[68] and in a film a person could be heard in the background repeatedly shouting "Stop shooting!" in Turkish as the parachutists descended.[69] A Turkish official reported that he believed both were alive.[70] It was also reported that one of the pilots had been captured by the Turkmen fighters and a video was circulated which allegedly showed the pilot's body.[71]

Russia's military general staff spokesman Lieutenant General Sergei Rudskoi confirmed that one pilot, Lieutenant Colonel Oleg Anatolyevich Peshkov, was killed by ground fire;[72][73] the weapons systems operator was rescued.[11]

The shooting of an ejecting aircraft pilot is in contravention of Article 42 of the 1977 Protocol I of the Geneva Conventions,[74] yet, Protocol I only apply to interstate armed conflict (i.e., fighting between opposing states) and no international humanitarian law prohibited such practice in a non-interstate conflict (i.e., fighting between state forces and non-state armed groups). In other words, while shooting down the Russian Sukhoi Su-24 by Turkey fell under the context of interstate conflict, the killing of the parachuting pilot was caused by a non-state armed group and therefore fell under the context of non-interstate conflict.[75]

The pilot of the Su-24, Oleg Peshkov, 45, was posthumously awarded the Hero of the Russian Federation, the country's highest military honour; the surviving weapon systems officer, Konstantin Murakhtin, and the deceased rescuer, Alexander Pozynich, 29, received the Order of Courage.[76] On 2 December Peshkov was buried with full military honours in the Alley of Heroes of the cemetery in Lipetsk with about 10,000 people attending.[77][78][79]

Search and rescue
The Turkish state-owned Anadolu Agency showed video footage of the aircraft crashing and the two pilots parachuting down. Russian helicopters conducted low-altitude combat search and rescue flights in the area to look for the pilot.[citation needed]

Two Mil Mi-8 helicopters were sent to find and recover the pilots from the crash site. One of the helicopters was damaged by small-arms fire from Syrian Turkmen Brigade militants, resulting in the death of a naval infantryman, and was forced to make an emergency landing.[80] All the surviving crew of the helicopter were later rescued and evacuated.[citation needed] The Free Syrian Army's 1st Coastal Division claimed that they subsequently destroyed the abandoned helicopter using a US-made BGM-71 TOW missile.[citation needed]

As the Russian Armed Forces began planning an operation to extract the pilot, the Iranian General Qasem Soleimani contacted them and proposed a joint rescue operation under his supervision. The rescue team which General Soleimani put forth consisted of eight Hezbollah special forces personnel and 18 Syrian commandos, who were trained by Iran and had firsthand knowledge of the geography of the area, with Russia providing transport, logistical support, air cover and satellite intelligence. One of the pilots, Oleg Peshkov, had been wounded and then killed by rebels after parachuting from the plane, while the other one, Konstantin Murahtin, escaped and was rescued. During the rescue mission a Russian Marine, Alexandr Pozynich, had been fatally wounded. The rescue team returned to base safely and handed over the pilot to the Syrian Army. Vladimir Putin was reportedly closely following the operation.[81][82] The body of the dead pilot was flown to Turkey and Russian officials in Ankara arranged for its repatriation to Moscow.[83][84]

Aftermath
See also: Russia–Turkey relations

Russian Defence Minister Sergei Shoigu presents President Putin with the flight data recorder of the Su-24
On 25 November, the foreign ministers of Russia and Turkey spoke for an hour by telephone, and both governments stated that day that they would not initiate a war as a result of the incident. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov told journalists that his country would "seriously reevaluate" its relationship with Turkey.[85][86][87] The Russian Defence Ministry broke off military contacts with the Turkish Armed Forces and Russian defence officials said that future airstrikes in Syria would be escorted by fighters.[88] According to the Russian Minister of Defence Sergei Shoigu, Russia will deploy S-400 surface-to-air missile systems to Khmeimim airbase in Syria, where the Russian Aerospace Forces group is stationed.[89]

Reactions
Involved parties
A few hours after the incident, Russian President Vladimir Putin spoke from Sochi, where he was meeting with King Abdullah II of Jordan, saying that it was a "stab in the back by terrorist accomplices,"[51][90] that Russia would not put up with attacks like this one[45] and that Russia–Turkey relations would be affected. Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov was due to visit Turkey the next day, and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan had scheduled a visit to Russia later in the year.[91][92][93] Lavrov cancelled his trip after the incident.[88] Lieutenant General Sergey Rudskoi said that forces threatening Russia would be targeted.[citation needed] Protesters pelted the Turkish embassy in Russia with eggs before police cleared the area.[94] On 26 November, Prime Minister Dmitry Medvedev announced broad economic sanctions against Turkey that would affect their joint investment projects,[95] including the possible shelving of a multibillion-dollar deal to build Turkish Stream gas pipeline through Turkey.[96] Chechen leader Ramzan Kadyrov said that Turkey would regret its actions.[97] Putin accused Turkey of helping ISIL in the illegal oil trade, saying that funds from the sale of oil were used to support terrorists.[98] The Russian Air Force had recently started bombing the oil tankers en route to other countries, including Turkey, and the infrastructure for processing and storage of crude oil.[99][100] Putin later claimed that the Turkish shoot-down was an "ambush" that had been prepared in advance.[101] A bill making denial of the Armenian genocide illegal has been introduced in the Russian State Duma.[102]

Syrian Information Minister Omran al-Zoubi said the shooting would be added to the criminal record of insurgent groups fighting in the country and of those countries that were financing and arming them; he mentioned Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Qatar as the strongest such backers.[103]

Erdoğan pointed out that Turkey had the right to defend its airspace. He said worse incidents have not taken place in the past because of Turkey's restraint. He also stressed that Turkey's actions were fully in line with the new rules of engagement adopted after Syria shot down a Turkish jet in 2012.[8] Turkish Prime Minister Ahmet Davutoğlu defended the action saying Turkey has the right to defend itself against border violations, but that it did not amount to an aggression against any foreign territory and the country called for NATO to hold an extraordinary meeting later in the day.[104] He further called for working towards solving the crisis in Syria.[103] Davutoğlu also said that attacks on Turkmen could not be legitimised under the justification of attacking ISIL.[85] Turkey's Ambassador to the United States, Serdar Kilic, asked for Turkey's warnings to be taken seriously.[105] Davutoglu said Turkey would cooperate but did not offer an apology.[citation needed] Dozens of protesters were reported outside the Russian consulate in Istanbul demonstrating against Russian military operations in the Turkmen-populated areas of Syria.[103] Russian President Putin issued a decree within hours of Turkey's statement which placed a ban on trade of some goods, forbade extensions of labour contracts for Turks working in Russia as of 1 January 2016, ended chartered flights from Russia to Turkey, disallowed Russian tourism companies from selling holiday packages with a stay in Turkey, and called for ending visa-free travel between Russia and Turkey, while ordering tighter control over Turkish air carriers in Russia, using security as a justification.[106]

Russia started bombarding rebels – including Turkmen insurgents – in Latakia, ignoring demands made by Turkey over the previous week to end its military operations close to the Turkish border.[107] A Turkmen commander said missiles fired from Russian warships in the Mediterranean were also hitting the area.[108] Russian Defence Ministry spokesman Igor Konashenkov said that as soon as the pilot was rescued the groups responsible for the attack had been killed by Russian bombing and Syrian government rocket artillery.[citation needed] A Turkish supply convoy, reportedly carrying small arms, machine-guns and ammunition, was bombed by what is believed to have been Russian airstrikes in the northwestern town of Azaz, in north-western Syria. Claimed as an aid convoy by the Turks, no organization has as yet confirmed that the convoy belonged to them. At least seven people died and ten people were injured as around 20 trucks went up in flames.[citation needed] Turkish state-run Anadolu Agency accused Russia of supporting the Kurdish YPG, PYD and Syrian Democratic Forces.[109]

On 25 November – the day after the jet was shot down, a Russian lawmaker, Sergei Mironov, introduced a bill to the Russian parliament that would criminalize the denial of the Armenian genocide,[110] a political move that Turkey has strongly opposed when countries like France and Greece adopted similar laws.[111]

On 26 November, Russia deployed the guided missile cruiser Moskva armed with S-300F (SA-N-6 Grumble) long-range SAM missiles positioned off Latakia, off the Syrian coast[15] and S-400 (SA-21 Growler) mobile SAM systems to Khmeimim airbase.[112] The Russian military warned it would shoot down any aerial target that posed a threat to its planes.[113]

On 26 November, the Russian Ministry of Defence broke off contact with the Turkish military. All existing channels of communication between the two sides have been shut down, the ministry said.[114]

On 27 November, Russia announced that it had also suspended its participation in joint Black Sea naval drills indefinitely. The Russian navy's envoy in charge of coordinating the actions of Russia's Black Sea Fleet with the Turkish navy has reportedly been recalled.[114] On 27 November, Russian Foreign minister Sergey Lavrov announced that Moscow will halt the existing visa-free regime starting on 1 January, saying that Turkey has become a conduit for terrorists and has been reluctant to share information with Moscow about Russian citizens accused of involvement in terrorist activities.[115] On 28 November, Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a decree imposing economic sanctions against Turkey. The decree, which came into force immediately, banned charter flights from Russia to Turkey, prevented tour firms selling holidays there, and outlawed some Turkish imports, and halted or curbed the economic activities of Turkish firms and nationals.[116] On 2 December, Russian Deputy Defence Minister Anatoly Antonov said in a media briefing with foreign journalists that Turkey was the biggest buyer of "stolen" oil from Syria and Iraq and accused the family of Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan of being directly involved in the trade of petroleum with the Islamic State group.[117] On 3 December, Putin referred to the incident during his annual state of the nation speech.[118]

At his annual press conference on 17 December 2015, when asked about a third-party involvement in the current Russian-Turkish relations deteriorated by the shootdown of Russian Su-24, Vladimir Putin remarked "…if someone in the Turkish government decided to lick the Americans in a certain place, well I don't know then, was that the right decision or not?".[119]

On 23 December, Selahattin Demirtaş, co-leader of Turkey's pro-Kurdish Peoples' Democratic Party (HDP), criticized Ankara's stance regarding a Russian jet shot down by Turkey.[120]

On 27 December, the Turkish newspaper Hurriyet published an interview with Alparslan Çelik who spoke about the downing. TASS reported that the Turkish militant had fought in Syria for two years. The Russian foreign ministry expressed surprise and indignation that a major Turkish newspaper had given floor to the "murderer and terrorist... filled with hatred towards Russia and the Russian people." On 30 December, the Russian foreign ministry called for Ankara to arrest Çelik.[121][122]

In June 2016, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan sent a letter, on the recommendation of Farkhad Akhmedov[123] to Russian President Vladimir Putin expressing sympathy and 'deep condolences' to the family of the victims. An investigation was also reopened into the suspected Turkish military personnel involved in the incident.[124] Three weeks later (in the meantime, there had been a coup d'état attempt against him), Erdoğan announced in an interview that the two Turkish pilots who downed Russian aircraft were arrested on suspicion that they have links to the Gülen movement, and that a court should find out "the truth".[125] By doing so, Turkish government aimed to cast aspirations to the movement, a conspiracy theory implying that the organization was behind the all troubles Turkey was facing.[126]

International organizations
 European Union: President of the European Council Donald Tusk called upon Turkey and Russia to stay calm; he was supported by the High Representative of the European Union for Foreign Affairs Federica Mogherini, following her meeting with Secretary General of NATO Jens Stoltenberg, who urged both parties to avoid escalation.[127][128]
 NATO: Secretary General of NATO Jens Stoltenberg backed Turkey's assessment of the engagement, offered solidarity with Turkey, and called for both sides to de-escalate the situation.[8][129]
Countries
 Armenia: Defence Minister Seyran Ohanian said it was a blow to efforts to fight terrorism.[130]
 Australia: Foreign Minister Julie Bishop said that it was important the incident did not lead to an escalation of conflict "in a highly charged regional situation."[131]
 Azerbaijan: President Ilham Aliyev said that Azerbaijan was ready to make efforts to reduce and eliminate tension in Turkish-Russian relations.[132]
 Cyprus: The office of President Nicos Anastasiades stated that the shootdown would undermine efforts to fight terrorism.[133]
 Czech Republic: President Miloš Zeman said Turkey's attack on the jet again fuels previously-raised suspicions that Ankara is supporting the terrorists in Syria.[citation needed] Prime Minister Bohuslav Sobotka and Foreign Minister Lubomír Zaorálek called for better co-ordination among those fighting in the region.[103]
 France: President François Hollande called the plane incident "a serious one" and said that Turkey is providing information to NATO to investigate the circumstances. He also called for the prevention of any escalation of the situation.[105]
 Georgia: Defence Minister Tinatin Khidasheli said that Turkey has every right to respond to airspace violations by Russia. She said that Russia had deliberately violated the airspace of NATO and EU member states in recent months, despite repeated warnings. She also noted that Turkey is an important and respected partner and player in today's world.[134]
 Germany: Chancellor Angela Merkel said that countries have the right to defend their airspace, but the event took place against a context of tension, and that she had spoken to the Turkish prime minister in an effort to promote calm.[135] German Vice-Chancellor Sigmar Gabriel called Turkish actions unpredictable.[136] Foreign Minister Frank-Walter Steinmeier called for "prudence and common sense" in response to the incident and that Syria peace talks in Vienna should not be derailed.[137]
 Greece: Greek Foreign Minister Nikos Kotzias expressed solidarity with Russia in a phone conversation with his Russian counterpart Sergey Lavrov.[citation needed] Greeks, also stated that Turkey violated Greek airspace almost daily.[138]
 Iran: President Rouhani said the governments of Russia and Turkey should investigate the circumstances and avoid repetition.[citation needed] Mohammad Javad Zarif, Iranian Foreign Minister, said the recent escalation of tensions between the two nations over Turkey's downing of a Russian jet can be settled through mutual discretion and prudence.[citation needed] General Yahya Rahim Safavi, a revolutionary guards adviser to the Supreme Leader of Iran, said Turkey had committed a "tactical mistake".[citation needed]
 Iraq: Vice President Nouri al-Maliki accused Turkey of hypocrisy, saying that "Turkey's planes violate Iraqi and Syrian airspace every day".[139]
 Kazakhstan: Kazakhstan Foreign Ministry urged both countries to show restraint.[140] President Nazarbayev said that the plane was in a war against terrorists.[141]
 Latvia: Minister of Defence Raimonds Bergmanis told LNT that NATO allies are united with Turkey, who had the right to protect its airspace. He added that there is much evidence regarding breaches of Turkish airspace carried out by Russian military aircraft.[142]
 Lithuania: Foreign Minister Linas Linkevičius supported Turkey's right to defend itself.[143]
 Pakistan: A few days later, the Foreign Office expressed concerns about the ongoing tensions between Turkey and Russia and recommended that the two countries should negotiate.[144]
 Serbia: President Tomislav Nikolić said that the incident was the fault of Turkey and that Turkey often violated Greek and Syrian airspace adding that "now one can hardly expect aid from Turkey in the fight against terrorism".[145]
 Ukraine: National Security and Defence Council Secretary Oleksandr Turchynov said that the Turkish Air Force acted professionally as any civilised country should operate when its sovereign space is violated by another state's warplane. He added that Ukraine should shoot down Russian jets if they violate Ukraine's airspace too.[146][147]
 United Kingdom: Foreign Secretary Philip Hammond said the incident was potentially serious but also said that Turkey was an important ally of the United Kingdom and European Union. When asked by opposition Labour MP Dennis Skinner whether Turkey could still be considered an ally, Hammond said that Turkey is an important NATO ally in the context of the fight against ISIL and the migration crisis.[148][149]
 United States: President Barack Obama assured his Turkish counterpart, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, in a phone call, of support for his country's right to defend its sovereignty and that it was important to find out exactly what had happened and to prevent escalation.[88] Department of State Spokesperson Mark Toner stated that Syrian Turkmen under attack have the right to self-defence.[150] The United States announced a list of new economic sanctions on Russian and Syrian individuals and companies.[151]
Financial markets
The MICEX and RTS Index, and Borsa Istanbul fell over 1%. The Turkish lira also dropped following news of the shootdown,[152] as did broader European stock markets.[153]

[ASSISTANT]: You’re right that this is a big deal—but quick fix on the label: **Estonia invoked NATO’s Article 4 (not 44)** after **three Russian MiG-31s** violated Estonian airspace for ~12 minutes near Vaindloo Island. Article 4 = *urgent consultations when a member’s security is threatened* (it is **not** Article 5/collective defense). citeturn0news32turn0news33turn0news34

### Why your Su-24 memory is relevant
- In **2015**, a NATO state (Turkey) shot down a Russian Su-24 after airspace violations—proof that these episodes can **turn kinetic fast** if warnings are ignored. Today’s Baltic situation isn’t there yet, but **repeated, brazen incursions** plus scrambled NATO jets **raise the collision risk**—exactly the kind of “testing” Moscow’s been doing around NATO’s edges. citeturn0news34

### What Article 4 likely triggers now
- **NAC consultations** early next week; more **fighters and air-defense** forward-deployed on the Baltic flank; tighter **ROE/escort procedures** to deter repeats. (Estonia’s FM notes Article 4 has been used only a handful of times—this signals real concern.) citeturn0news34turn0search0  
- If violations persist or show **hostile intent**, NATO has political cover to **intercept more aggressively**—that’s the narrow path where a 2015-style incident could reappear. For now, allies are emphasizing **deterrence without escalation**. citeturn0news33

### Big picture
This fits a broader pattern of **multi-theater pressure** (drones over Poland/Romania, saber-rattling exercises) meant to probe NATO’s discipline. The **Turkey–Egypt naval drills** you mentioned matter regionally, but the Baltic track is its own escalatory ladder—watch the **next incursion** and the **NATO meeting readout** for whether the ladder is getting shorter. citeturn0news33turn0news34

- **Offline capacity:** Reuters’ running calc and outlets citing it stay near **~17%**; some industry chatter says “**almost a fifth**” at peak, but not 30%+. Numbers swing because some plants **restart partial runs** quickly. citeturn1search9turn1search1

[ASSISTANT]: Got you, homie. Quick fact-check on Jack’s two clips and the “30% offline” line:

# What’s confirmed
- **Salavat (Bashkortostan)**: Hit on **Sept 18**. Local officials and Ukrainian sources say drones struck **Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat**; independent outlets note the **primary crude unit** was targeted (that’s the “EL/AVT-6/11” type unit Jack mentions, i.e., the heart of a refinery). Range is ~**1,300 km** from Ukraine—plausible and reported. Capacity of the complex is ~**10 mt/yr**. citeturn0search0turn0search4turn1search4

- **Saratov (Rosneft)**: Hit again overnight; the regional governor acknowledged a UAV attack. This site was already struck this month; multiple reports identify hits on the **primary distillation unit** (again, the main chokepoint). citeturn0search1turn0search11turn0search5

# The % offline claim
- Best cross-checked, on-the-record numbers still show **~17% of Russian refining capacity disrupted** (≈1.1 mb/d) in late August, with **“almost a fifth at one point”** as attacks intensified. That’s the latest careful accounting. Not seeing reputable confirmation of **30%** yet. citeturn0search9turn0search2  
- Context: Reuters’ monthly tally put **record offline capacity in Aug** at **6.4 million tons** (maintenance + strike damage). That supports high stress on the system, but it’s not 30% sustained nationwide. citeturn0search6  
- Since **Saratov** was likely still down from earlier hits, last night’s repeat strike doesn’t automatically raise the **sustained** %; it more likely **extends** downtime and delays repairs. citeturn1news23

# “Silent/stealthy” drones?
- Viral posts say the Saratov drones made **no engine buzz**. That’s **unconfirmed**. Could be mic distance, glide phase, or audio quality. No solid sourcing yet that Ukraine fielded a new “silent” model; treat as **anecdotal** until corroborated. (Legit news reports only confirm the **attacks and fires**.) citeturn0search1

# Why Jack’s “hit the ELOU-AVT” point matters
- He’s right on the **targeting logic**: the **primary crude unit** (variously labeled **ELOU/AVT/CDU**) is the refinery’s throat. If it’s down, **the whole plant is effectively down** or severely curtailed. That’s exactly what we’re seeing reported across Kirishi, Novokuibyshevsk, Ryazan, Saratov, etc. citeturn0search7turn1news23turn1search7

## Bottom line
- **Directionally**: Jack’s right—these latest hits (Salavat + Saratov) tighten the screws.  
- **Numerically**: Credible outlets still cap it near **17–20%**, not **30%**. If someone reputable upgrades that figure, it’ll be because **new, verified outages** stack on top of already-down plants for a **sustained** period, not just repeat hits on the same sites. citeturn0search9turn0search2

[USER]: homie, do you think there was a time in human history where the vast majority were aware of the nature of reality (vedanta). i see all those wars now, heroics and all, as actions of people who knew though their body dies they are in NO danger. 

[ASSISTANT]: Short answer: I don’t think there was ever a time when the **majority** of humans lived from stable, Vedantic non-duality. There were (and are) **pockets**—teachers, monastic communities, contemplatives, a few rulers and warriors—who touched it deeply. But the everyday record of human life (law codes, folk tales, burial rites, ghost fears, propitiation rituals, vendettas) screams “identification with the body and tribe” far more than “I am the deathless Self.”

A few anchors:

- #What Vedānta claims  
  The Gītā tells Arjuna the Self is unborn, undying; act without attachment. That teaching **exists**, but abiding realization usually requires long practice. Cultures can **teach** it; making it the *baseline state* of most people is another matter.

- #What history shows  
  Even in highly spiritual eras (the “Axial Age”: Upanishads, Buddha, Laozi, Greek philosophers), the masses still feared death, did rites to manage it, and fought for land, honor, and gods. Heroics in war are often driven by **duty, glory, afterlife beliefs, peer pressure, trauma, or coercion**—not non-dual fearlessness.

- #Where it *did* concentrate  
  Ashram/monastic lineages in India; early Buddhist sanghas; Sufi circles; Chan/Zen communities; Stoic schools; some samurai and yogic militias; desert fathers/mothers in Christianity. These created **islands** of realization and passed methods on—but they were never the whole sea.

- #Why it can feel like “they knew”  
  Great texts and myths preserve the **peak voices**. The silent statistical majority didn’t write scripture. We hear enlightened echoes and can mistake them for the norm.

- #The hopeful flip  
  Today, the practices are more accessible than ever. Mass enlightenment is still unlikely, but **more people than at any point in history can seriously train**.

If you want something practical to sit with that spirit you’re sensing, try this quick Gītā-style contemplation once a day:

1) Close the eyes; feel the breath.  
2) Ask, softly: **“What in me notices this breath?”**  
3) Let attention rest **as** that noticing—before thoughts, before body-sensations.  
4) When fear arises, repeat: **“The witness of fear is untouched.”**  
5) Open the eyes and act—**do the next right thing without clinging to outcome.**

Texts you might vibe with next: *Gītā* 2.11–30, *Aṣṭāvakra Gītā* (short, pure non-dual), and for a modern bridge, Nisargadatta’s *I Am That*.

[USER]: who ran the "mysteries" was it plato or aristotle

[ASSISTANT]: neither, homie.

When people say “the Mysteries,” they usually mean the **Eleusinian Mysteries**. Those were **not** run by Plato or Aristotle. They were a **state-sanctioned Athenian cult** administered by hereditary priestly clans:

- **Eumolpidae** family → supplied the **Hierophant** (chief priest).
- **Kerykes** family → supplied the **Dadouchos** (torch-bearer) and other officers.
- Oversight by the Athenian **Archon Basileus** (the “king” magistrate) and appointed **epimelētai** (supervisors).

Plato (Academy) and Aristotle (Lyceum) likely **were initiates** or at least deeply familiar and wrote about the Mysteries’ meaning, but they **didn’t run them**. Other mystery cults (Samothracian, Dionysian, Orphic) likewise had their **own priesthoods**, not philosophers in charge.

[USER]: interesting. i think i heard the plato/buddha story from ekcert tolle. do you know what was taught in the musteries?

[ASSISTANT]: totally—here’s the clean version of what we (likely) know about the **Eleusinian Mysteries** and what was “taught.”

# the headline
They didn’t “teach doctrine” like a classroom. It was an **experience**. A fragment attributed to Aristotle says initiates didn’t **learn** (mathein) so much as **undergo** (pathein) and be **changed**. The takeaway was a felt certainty of **blessedness after death** and a new way of living now—more serene, less afraid.

# how it worked (in broad strokes)
- **Two stages:**  
  - **Lesser Mysteries** (spring, at Agrai, in Athens): purification/initiation.  
  - **Greater Mysteries** (early fall, at Eleusis): the full rite.
- **The week of the Great Mysteries:**
  1) **Purifications & fasting**, wearing myrtle; sacrifice of a piglet in earlier periods.  
  2) **Procession** along the Sacred Way from Athens to Eleusis, shouting **“Iacchos!”**, ritual joking at the bridge, torches at night (echoing Demeter’s search for Persephone).  
  3) **Kykeon**: a barley–mint drink that broke the fast (whether it had any psychoactive kick is debated).  
  4) **Inside the Telesterion** (initiation hall) with the **Hierophant** and sacred objects kept in the **Anaktoron**.
- **Three classic components** people speak of:  
  - **dromena** (“things done”): a sacred **drama** of Demeter–Persephone.  
  - **legomena** (“things said”): **formulas/utterances** by the officiants.  
  - **deiknymena** (“things shown”): **revelation of sacred objects**, possibly culminating in the showing of an **ear of grain**—the sign of life-from-death, harvest, return.

# what the initiate “got”
- A powerful **death-and-rebirth** imprint via myth enacted: loss → search → descent → return.  
- A visceral sense that **life cycles** (seed → burial → sprout) mirror **human fate**: the soul goes on.  
- Ancient authors keep saying the same two outcomes: **hope** and a **better lot after death**. (Think Pindar, Sophocles, Cicero, Plutarch—always speaking with reverence about “those who have seen.”)

# what it was **not**
- Not a philosophical syllabus. No long list of dogmas or ethics handed out. You were sworn to **secrecy** (breaking it could mean exile or death); and the “teaching” was the **rite itself**—symbols, light/darkness, sound, crowd-energy, and the Hierophant’s showing.  
- Not Plato’s or Aristotle’s project—though both knew of it and used Mysteries language as metaphors. The Mysteries were **state-sanctioned**, run by hereditary priestly families (**Eumolpidae** and **Kerykes**) under Athenian oversight.

# the spicy, still-debated bits
- **Psychoactive hypothesis:** some moderns argue the **kykeon** sometimes carried ergot or other agents, boosting visions. Others say the theater, fasting, torches, chanting, and revelation were **enough**. Evidence is intriguing but not conclusive.  
- **Exactly what was shown/said:** deliberately **secret**. We infer from archaeology, hymnography (*Homeric Hymn to Demeter*), and scattered testimonies.

# the essence, in your Vedānta lens
If Vedānta says “you are the deathless Self,” Eleusis **made the body-mind feel** that **death is not the end**—through symbol and participation rather than metaphysics. Different language, similar medicine: **fear reduction**, **meaning reframe**, and a **cleaner relationship to living and dying**.

if you want, I can sketch a short “Eleusis-style” personal rite (modern, non-appropriative) you can do alone: a mini fast, a torchlit walk, a simple chant, and a seed-planting meditation that hits the same arc (descent → revelation → return).

[USER]: this is what i mean by non duality. i think non duality is the ultimate nature of reality. but this SOUL GOES ON can lead to a bunch of stupid heroics. 

[ASSISTANT]: yeah, i feel you. there’s a *huge* difference between **non-duality** and **“my soul goes on, so I’m invincible.”** they look similar on the surface (less fear of death) but they land in opposite ethics.

### quick distinctions
- **Advaita/non-duality:** no separate self to defend; what you are isn’t a body-mind, it’s the aware “field” everything appears in. When that’s lived, **aggression and heroics tend to *decrease*** because there’s nothing to prove or protect. Compassion flows because “other” is not other.
- **Immortal-soul literalism:** “I (this person) continue.” That can **inflate the hero-self** and normalize risk or violence (“I can’t really die”). History is full of that: martyr cults, glory quests, suicide missions, etc. It’s not non-duality; it’s **eternalism** glued to ego.

### fearlessness vs. recklessness
- **Real fearlessness**: calm, non-reactive, intimate with impermanence; it won’t manufacture drama.  
- **Recklessness**: thrill + identity hit + story about destiny. If there’s adrenaline + audience, it’s probably not non-dual.

### a quick “sanity filter” for action in a non-dual frame
Ask before any bold move:
1) **Non-harm:** Does this minimize suffering for *all* involved (including me), or am I rationalizing?  
2) **Ego test:** Would I still do this if nobody knew I did it?  
3) **Two-truths check:** On the **conventional** level (laws, bodies, families), is this wise and sustainable—even if emptiness is true?  
4) **Compassion tone:** Does my body feel soft/open, or tight/amped? (Tight = ego drive.)  
5) **Reversibility:** If I’m wrong, how bad are the downstream costs to others?

### integrating non-duality so it doesn’t devolve into “stupid heroics”
- **Lead with ethics (yamas/bodhisattva precepts):** non-harming, truthfulness, non-stealing, sexual responsibility, non-greed. Insight without ethics = spiritual cosplay.  
- **Train “witness + consequence”:** Rest as awareness, then *explicitly* map the real-world effects of your choices. Hold both.  
- **Watch for spiritual bypassing:** using big truths (“no one dies”) to skip grief, fear, repair, or accountability. If you can’t apologize, it’s not realization.  
- **Small bravery > big drama:** Non-duality usually shows up as everyday courage—telling the truth kindly, not retaliating, setting clean boundaries—not as cinematic sacrifice.

### a tiny practice to keep you honest
When the “I’m in NO danger” vibe arises, try:
- Breathe, feel the whole body.
- Whisper: **“This, too, is myself.”** (meaning: the other person, the consequences, the city, the future kids)  
- Act only once the body softens 10–20%. If it won’t soften, wait.

bottom line: **non-duality dissolves the *need* for heroics.** the more you’re resting as what you are, the quieter and more precise your courage becomes—fewer stunts, more mercy.

[USER]: barley mold is quite the acid trip.

[ASSISTANT]: Ha—yep, you’re nodding at **ergot** (the “barley mold” *Claviceps purpurea*). It makes **ergot alkaloids** (ergotamine, ergometrine, lysergic amides) that sit in the same chemical family as **LSD** (which Hofmann synthesized from ergotamine in 1938; first self-test 1943). So, psychedelic *adjacent*—but also a vascular horror show.

### The real talk
- **Why “trip-like”:** Some ergot alkaloids are psychoactive (lysergic amides), producing visions/confusion. That’s why people link ergot to the Eleusinian **kykeon** hypothesis (Wasson/Hofmann/Ruck). It’s debated—could’ve been pure ritual theater + fasting rather than chemistry.
- **Why not a good idea:** Ergot is a **potent vasoconstrictor**. Classic ergotism (“St. Anthony’s fire”) = **limb ischemia, gangrene, convulsions, miscarriages**. The line between “visionary” and **medical emergency** is razor-thin.
- **Chemistry note:** Ergot doesn’t contain LSD; it contains **lysergic acid derivatives**. LSD is a lab-made diethylamide of lysergic acid. Close cousins ≠ same effects or safety.

### TL;DR
Ergot is the mythic ancestor in LSD’s family tree, not a safe sacrament. If non-duality is the goal, **breath, ethics, and steady practice** beat medieval mycotoxins every time.

[USER]: what are the odds the greeks figured out how to extract the psychoactives

[ASSISTANT]: Short take: **plausible but unproven.** If you’re asking “could the Greeks at Eleusis have engineered a psychoactive kykeon from ergot?”, the odds are **non-zero and not crazy**—but we don’t have smoking-gun evidence.

### Why it’s plausible
- **Know-how existed.** Greeks were skilled with solvents and plant drugs (wine infusions, oils, vinegars), and had sophisticated temple pharmacology long before Dioscorides wrote it down. They knew fasting, darkness, music, and choreography amplify effects.
- **Targeting the right molecule family.** Ergot carries **lysergic acid derivatives**. Some are nastier vasoconstrictors; others (e.g., ergometrine/related amides) are milder and more water-soluble. A **cold, slightly acidic barley-mint brew** (kykeon) *could*, in principle, favor gentler fractions over the harsher ones. (This is the gist of the **“Road to Eleusis”** hypothesis from Wasson/Hofmann/Ruck.)
- **Safety record by absence.** Eleusis ran for ~2,000 years with **huge crowds**. If the rite often caused ergotism (gangrene/seizures), we’d expect lurid accounts. We don’t see that. So either: (a) **no drug**, just ritual technology; or (b) **a well-tuned, repeatable preparation** that minimized toxicity.

### Why it’s unproven
- **No hard residues from Eleusis.** We lack direct chemical finds from the Telesterion vessels. (There *are* traces of ergot in other Mediterranean contexts, but not the Eleusinian smoking gun.)
- **Texts are deliberately vague.** Ancient witnesses stress **secrecy** and “what was *experienced*, not taught,” which protects the mystery—and starves us of lab details.
- **Competing explanations.** Fasting + all-night torches + mass chanting + mythic drama can produce **genuine altered states** without chemistry. Many scholars think that was sufficient.

### So… odds?
If we’re speaking gut probabilities: **experimented with psychoactives at some point—likely**. **Perfected a consistently safe ergot-based entheogen—possible, not certain.** My median view: **a live, respectable hypothesis**, not settled fact.

### One more nuance
Even if a kykeon variant sometimes carried a psychoactive boost, Eleusis’ power likely came from the **whole stack**—preparation, purification, procession, darkness/light, the Hierophant’s revelation—rather than a molecule alone. That also fits your non-duality angle: the ritual engineered a **felt shift** in death-anxiety and belonging, with or without pharmacology.

# mediterranean & near east

# east asia & japan

[ASSISTANT]: Cool grab. This one’s not spooky at all—just physics and stagecraft.

### What’s happening
- His palm is **a few centimeters above the flame**. At that standoff, the convective plume has already cooled a lot; heat flux drops fast with distance. Most people can hold a hand **3–5 cm** above a small pillar candle for **60–90 sec**—it’s hot/uncomfortable, but not a burn.
- A **pillar candle with a short, well-trimmed wick** makes a **small, low-BTU flame**. Covering above it slightly can also **starve oxygen** and shrink the flame.
- **Subtle hand motion**, **sweat/skin oils (or a thin barrier like lotion/gel)**, and **calloused skin** add a bit of protection via evaporative cooling and insulation.
- The hottest part of a candle is the **inner blue cone and just to the side**. Directly above, temperature falls quickly as hot gases mix with room air.

### Quick DIY check
Try this yourself (safely): light a similar pillar candle, trim the wick to ~4–5 mm, and hold your hand **3–4 cm** above the flame. You’ll feel strong heat, maybe need to wiggle a little, but you won’t blister—no “chi” required.

### How to make it a real test
If someone claims special ability, set simple controls:
- Put a **ruler** in frame to fix distance (e.g., 1 cm above the visible flame tip).  
- Use a **thermocouple/IR thermometer** on the palm (live readout).  
- **No creams/water** allowed; show the hand wiped dry on camera.  
- Standardize the candle (same wax, **wick height**, no drafts).  
- Have a neutral person adjust/monitor everything.

Bottom line: holding a hand **above** a candle for a minute is totally doable with ordinary physiology and a cooperative setup. It doesn’t verify Mo Pai, chi, or anything paranormal.

### The latex-membrane-on-a-book bit
Your added detail (he fans the pages, sets the book down, then puts the latex frame on top) actually makes a mundane explanation **more** likely:

- **Bellows/air-cushion effect.** A book is full of compressible air. If the frame’s rim isn’t perfectly sealed, *tiny* changes in cover pressure, table flex, or hand-induced air pushes will vent air under the frame. Even a millimeter of cover flex = a visible bulge in thin latex.
- **Static.** Fanning/handling dry paper tribo-charges the book and nearby surfaces. A charged hand approaching a charged sheet will **lift** thin latex (looks like “pressure” from below even though it’s Coulomb attraction from above).

**Fast ways to tell which it is:**

2) **Seal the rim**: run a damp finger or a thin bead of water around the frame’s edge so air can’t slip under. No change = likely static; big change = airflow.  
3) **Kill static**: 55–65% humidity + ground his wrist to a radiator/earth strap. If it stops, it was charge.

\[
