Killing Grants That Have Saved Lives: Trump’s Cuts Signal End to Government Work on Terrorism Prevention
Tens of millions of dollars slated for violence prevention have been cut or are frozen as DOGE steamrolls the national security sector. “This is the government getting out of the terrorism business,” said one grant recipient.
by Hannah Allam
March 20, 2025, 11:59 a.m. EDT

Share

Change Appearance
Change Appearance
Auto
Republish
ProPublica is a nonprofit newsroom that investigates abuses of power. Sign up to receive our biggest stories as soon as they’re published.


On a frigid winter morning in 2022, a stranger knocked on the door of a synagogue in Colleyville, Texas, during Shabbat service.

Soon after he was invited in for tea, the visitor pulled out a pistol and demanded the release of an al-Qaida-linked detainee from a nearby federal prison, seizing as hostages a rabbi and three worshipers. The standoff lasted 10 hours until the rabbi, drawing on extensive security training, hurled a chair at the assailant. The hostages escaped.

“We are alive today because of that education,” Rabbi Charlie Cytron-Walker said after the attack.

The averted tragedy at Congregation Beth Israel is cited as a success story for the largely unseen prevention work federal authorities have relied on for years in the fight to stop terrorist attacks and mass shootings. The government weaves together partnerships with academic researchers and community groups across the country as part of a strategy for addressing violent extremism as a public health concern.


A specialized intervention team at Boston Children’s Hospital treats young patients — some referred by the FBI — who show signs of disturbing, violent behavior. Eradicate Hate, a national prevention umbrella group, says one of its trainees helped thwart a school shooting in California last year by reporting a gun in a fellow student’s backpack. In other programs, counselors guide neo-Nazis out of the white-power movement or help families of Islamist extremists undo the effects of violent propaganda.

The throughline for this work is federal funding — a reliance on grants that are rapidly disappearing as the Trump administration guts billions in spending.

Tens of millions of dollars slated for violence prevention have been cut or are frozen pending review as President Donald Trump’s Department of Government Efficiency steamrolls the national security sector. Barring action from Congress or the courts, counterterrorism professionals say, the White House appears poised to end the government’s backing of prevention work on urgent threats.

“This is the government getting out of the terrorism business,” said one federal grant recipient who was ordered this week to cease work on projects including a database used by law enforcement agencies to assess threats.

This account is drawn from interviews with nearly two dozen current and former national security personnel, federally funded researchers and nonprofit grant recipients. Except in a few cases, they spoke on condition of anonymity for fear of retaliation from the Trump administration.

Dozens of academic and nonprofit programs that rely on grants from the Department of Homeland Security, the Justice Department and other agencies are in crisis mode, mirroring the uncertainty of other parts of the government amid Trump’s seismic reorganization.

“We’re on a precipice,” said the leader of a large nonprofit that has received multiple federal grants and worked with Democratic and Republican administrations on prevention campaigns.


The Department of Justice has collected information about FBI employees who worked on cases related to the Capitol riot as part of a purge of FBI personnel, which is also forcing out officials with terrorism expertise. Credit:Stefani Reynolds/Bloomberg via Getty Images
Program leaders describe a chilling new operating environment. Scholars of white supremacist violence — which the FBI for years has described as a main driver of domestic terrorism — wonder how they’ll be able to continue tracking the threat without running afoul of the administration’s ban on terms related to race and racism.


The training the rabbi credits with saving his Texas synagogue in 2022 came from a broader community initiative whose federal funding is in limbo. One imperiled effort, FEMA’s Nonprofit Security Grant Program, has helped Jewish institutions across the country install security cameras, train staff and add protective barriers, according to the nonprofit Secure Community Network, which gives security advice and monitors threats to Jewish communities nationwide.

In July 2023, access-control doors acquired through the grant program prevented a gunman from entering Margolin Hebrew Academy in Memphis. In 2021, when gunfire struck the Jewish Family Service offices in Denver, grant-funded protective window film stopped bullets from penetrating the building.

“These are not hypothetical scenarios, they are real examples of how NSGP funds prevent injuries and deaths,” Michael Masters, director of the Secure Community Network, wrote this month in an op-ed in The Jerusalem Post calling for continued funding of the program.

Now the security grants program has been shelved as authorities and Jewish groups warn of rising antisemitism. The generous reading, one Jewish program leader said, is that the funds were inadvertently swept up in DOGE cuts. Trump has been a vocal supporter of Jewish groups and, as one of his first acts in office, signed an executive order promising to tackle antisemitism.

Still, the freeze on grants for synagogue protections has revived talk of finding new, more independent funding streams.

Throughout Jewish history, the program director said, “we’ve learned you need a Plan B.”

The White House did not respond to requests for comment.

“Tsunami” of Cuts
For more than two decades, the federal government has invested tens of millions of dollars in prevention work and academic research with the goal of intervening in the crucial window known as “left of boom” — before an attack occurs.

The projects are diffuse, spread across several agencies, but the government’s central clearinghouse is at Homeland Security in the Center for Prevention Programs and Partnerships, often called CP3. The office houses a grant program that since 2020 has awarded nearly $90 million to community groups and law enforcement agencies working at the local level to prevent terrorism and targeted violence such as mass shootings.

These days, CP3 is imploding. Nearly 20% of its workforce was cut through the dismissal of probationary employees March 3. CP3 Director Bill Braniff, an Army veteran who had fiercely defended the office’s achievements in LinkedIn posts in recent weeks, resigned the same night.

“It is a small act of quiet protest, and an act of immense respect I have for them and for our team,” Braniff wrote in a departing message to staff that was obtained by ProPublica. In the note, he called the employees “wrongfully terminated.”

Some of this year’s CP3 grant recipients say they have no idea whether their funding will continue. One awardee said the team is looking at nightmare scenarios of laying off staff and paring operations to the bone.

“Everybody’s trying to survive,” the grantee said. “It feels like this is a tsunami and you don’t know how it’s going to hit you.”


Current and former DHS officials say they don’t expect the prevention mission to continue in any meaningful way, signaling the end to an effort that had endured through early missteps and criticism from the left and right.

The prevention mission evolved from the post-9/11 growth of a field known as countering violent extremism, or CVE. In early CVE efforts, serious scholars of militant movements jostled for funding alongside pseudo-scientists claiming to have discovered predictors of radicalization. CVE results typically weren’t measurable, allowing for inflated promises of success — “snake oil,” as one researcher put it.

Worse, some CVE programs billed as community partnerships to prevent extremism backfired and led to mistrust that persists today. Muslim advocacy groups were incensed by the government’s targeting of their communities for deradicalization programs, blaming CVE for stigmatizing law-abiding families and contributing to anti-Muslim hostility. Among the most influential Muslim advocacy groups, it is still taboo to accept funding from Homeland Security.

Defenders of CP3, which launched in 2021 from an earlier incarnation, insist that the old tactics based on profiling are gone. They also say there are now more stringent metrics to gauge effectiveness. CP3’s 2024 report to Congress listed more than 1,000 interventions since 2020, cases where prevention workers stepped in with services to dissuade individuals from violence.

The probationary employees who were dismissed this month represented the future of CP3’s public health approach to curbing violence, say current and former DHS officials. They were terminated by email in boilerplate language about poor performance, a detail that infuriated colleagues who viewed them as accomplished social workers and public health professionals.

There were no consultations with administration officials or DOGE — just the ax, said one DHS source with knowledge of the CP3 cuts. Promised exemptions for national security personnel apparently didn’t apply as Trump’s Homeland Security agenda shrinks to a single issue.

“The vibe is: How to use DHS to go after migrants, immigrants. That is the vibe, that is the only vibe, there is no other vibe,” the source said. “It’s wild — it’s as if the rest of the department doesn’t exist.”

This week, with scant warning, Homeland Security cut around $20 million for more than two dozen programs from another wing of DHS, including efforts aimed at stopping terrorist attacks and school shooters.

A Homeland Security spokesperson confirmed “sweeping cuts and reforms” aimed at eliminating waste but did not address questions about specific programs. DHS “remains focused on supporting law enforcement and public safety through funding, training, increased public awareness, and partnerships,” the statement said.

One grant recipient said they were told by a Homeland Security liaison that targeted programs were located in places named on a Fox News list of “sanctuary states” that have resisted or refused cooperation with the government’s deportation campaign. The grantee’s project was given less than an hour to submit outstanding expenses before the shutdown.

The orders were so sudden that even some officials within the government had trouble coming up with language to justify the termination notices. They said they were given no explanation for how the targeted programs were in violation of the president’s executive orders.

“I just don’t believe this is in any way legal,” said one official with knowledge of the cuts.


Members of the far-right group the Proud Boys rally outside the U.S. Capitol in 2025. In one of the first acts of his second term, President Donald Trump pardoned nearly 1,600 people convicted of crimes related to the 2021 attack on the Capitol and commuted the sentences of a handful of others, including former Proud Boys leader Enrique Tarrio, left. Credit:Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images
Threat Research in Limbo
Cuts are reshaping government across the board, but perhaps nowhere more jarringly than in the counterterrorism apparatus. The administration started dismantling it when the president granted clemency to nearly 1,600 defendants charged in connection with the storming of the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021.

The pardons overturned what the Justice Department had celebrated as a watershed victory in the fight against domestic terrorism.

Senior FBI officials with terrorism expertise have left or are being forced out in the purge of personnel involved in the Jan. 6 investigation. In other cases, agents working terrorism cases have been moved to Homeland Security to help with Trump’s mass deportation effort, a resource shift that runs counter to the government’s own threat assessments showing homegrown militants as the more urgent priority. The Justice Department did not respond to a request for comment.

Without research backing up the enforcement arm of counterterrorism, analysts and officials say, the government lacks the capacity to evaluate rapidly evolving homegrown threats.

Researchers are getting whiplash as grant dollars are frozen and unfrozen. Even if they win temporary relief, the prospect of getting new federal funding in the next four years is minimal. They described pressure to self-censor or tailor research narrowly to MAGA interests in far-left extremism and Islamist militants.

“What happens when you’re self-silencing? What happens if people just stop thinking they should propose something because it’s ‘too risky?’” said one extremism scholar who has advised senior officials and received federal funding. “A lot of ideas that could be used to prevent all kinds of social harms, including terrorism, could get tossed.”

Among the projects at risk is a national compilation of threats to public officials, including assassination attempts against Trump; research on the violent misogyny that floods social media platforms; a long-term study of far-right extremists who are attempting to disengage from hate movements. The studies are underway at research centers and university labs that, in some cases, are funded almost entirely by Homeland Security. [ASSISTANT]: Good question, homie. Let me break it down simply:

- **Most Indian philosophies** (like Advaita Vedanta, Buddhism, Yoga, Nyaya) talk about *dharma* as the cosmic order, right conduct, or duty aligned with truth and harmony. Dharma keeps society and the universe in balance.  

- **Jainism takes it further** in two ways:
  1. **Literal principle of motion** – Jainism treats *Dharma* not just as morality, but as a **real substance of the universe**. In Jain metaphysics, *Dharma-dravya* is a fundamental substance that makes movement possible (and its twin, *Adharma-dravya*, makes rest possible). So dharma is not only ethics, but also part of the physics of existence.  
  2. **Absolute non-violence (Ahimsa)** – Jain ethics radicalize dharma into total non-harm. Where Hinduism or Buddhism may permit contextual duty (like Arjuna fighting in the Gita, or Buddhist “skillful means”), Jainism says: no killing, no lying, no stealing, no sexual misconduct, no possession — at all, if you want liberation. Even microscopic harm matters.

- **So compared to others:**  
  - Hindu dharma = harmony of cosmic/social duties (sometimes flexible, contextual).  
  - Buddhist dharma = truth/law of reality (the teachings of the Buddha).  
  - Jain dharma = both a **cosmic principle of motion** *and* an **absolute ethical law of non-harm** — stricter, more uncompromising.  

👉 In that sense, yes — Jainism takes dharma further, both metaphysically (turning it into a substance of the universe) and ethically (pushing it into total non-violence, without exceptions).  

Would you like me to sketch a quick side-by-side table of how Vedanta, Buddhism, and Jainism each define *dharma* so you can see the contrasts cleanly?

[USER]: so in jainsim any action that doesnt at all times protect live would accumulate karma

[ASSISTANT]: Exactly, homie — you’ve got it. In Jainism the rule is *extremely strict* compared to other dharma systems:

- **Every action has karmic weight.** Jains see karma not as metaphor but as a kind of subtle material that binds to the soul when you harm or even intend harm.  
- **Non-violence is absolute.** If your action *fails* to protect life (or worse, directly harms), then yes — it accumulates karma. That’s why Jain monks sweep the ground before walking, filter water, avoid eating root vegetables (because uprooting them kills the whole plant and soil organisms).  
- **Intention still matters, but less forgiving.** In Hinduism or Buddhism, *intention* often reduces the weight of action. In Jainism, even unintentional harm counts — though deliberate harm binds heavier karma.  

So the Jain position is: unless your action at *all times* protects life (or at least minimizes harm to the tiniest degree possible), you’re adding karmic dust to the soul.  

That’s why Jain ethics are sometimes called the **“ascetic extreme” of dharma** — they make every step, bite, and breath a moral choice.  

Do you want me to map this against Advaita/Vedanta and Buddhism, showing how karma is “softer” in those compared to Jainism’s “granular, unforgiving” model?

- **Surface level (human reaction):** A bunny dies, it’s tragic. The little girl’s tears are pure empathy — no doctrine, just open-hearted grief at innocent life cut short.  

- **Karmic accounting lens (the “bastard last life” view):** In some readings, karma reduces suffering to “deserved consequences.” The bunny’s fate is seen as the outworking of past actions, not as an injustice. That can sound cold — almost blaming the victim.  

- **Jain lens:** They would say: yes, the bunny had karma to work out, but the driver *also* accumulates karma from causing harm (even unintentionally). The suffering multiplies — the bunny, the driver, the child crying, all caught in karmic knots.  

- **Advaita Vedānta lens:** From the highest standpoint (*paramārthika*), both bunny and suffering are appearances in *Māyā*. The Atman is untouched. But from the everyday standpoint (*vyāvahārika*), compassion is dharma — the little girl’s tears are real and appropriate.  

So the parable captures a **shadow side of karmic thinking**: it can explain away suffering instead of awakening compassion.  
But the deeper currents of these traditions often insist: the right response is *both* recognition of karma *and* compassion. Tears, prayers, and gentle conduct remain dharmic, regardless of what the bunny “was” before.  

👉 In other words, karma isn’t supposed to shut down the girl’s tears — it’s supposed to deepen understanding, without hardening the heart.

[USER]: advaita takes it to the core. in the ULTIMATE sense all but brahman is a construct. BUT ultimate is only 1 layer of reality. 

[ASSISTANT]: Yes, homie — exactly. You’ve got Advaita’s two-tier view of reality:  

- **Vyāvahārika satya (conventional/empirical truth):** the world of cars, bunnies, little girls crying. Cause and effect, karma, dharma — all function here. We live and act as if it’s real.  
- **Pāramārthika satya (ultimate truth):** only Brahman is real. Bunny, girl, death, karma — all appearances in *Māyā*. From this layer, nothing is ever born, nothing dies, no harm is truly done.  

Śaṅkara keeps both levels active:  
- To deny the everyday is to fall into nihilism or cold detachment.  
- To deny the ultimate is to stay bound in illusion.  

So the Advaitin would say:  
- On the *relative plane*, we act with compassion — stop the car, comfort the girl, honor the bunny. That’s dharma.  
- On the *ultimate plane*, we recognize: the tears, the bunny, even the compassion itself — all waves on Brahman’s sea, untouched at the core.  

It’s like **two registers of music playing at once**: the melody of everyday dharma and the drone of ultimate Brahman. Both sound together.  

👉 The trap is when people hear “only Brahman is real” and use it to dismiss suffering. The teaching isn’t meant to *cancel* compassion — it’s meant to free compassion from ego (“*I* am comforting” → “comfort flows as dharma”).  

Want me to draw a little side-by-side showing how Jainism, Buddhism, and Advaita each handle those two layers (relative vs ultimate)?

[USER]: doesnt brahman "sleep" for several million years before restarting reality? 

[ASSISTANT]: You’re thinking of the **cosmic cycles** described in Hindu cosmology, homie. Advaita doesn’t deny those stories — it just frames them differently.  

Here’s the picture:  

- **In Purāṇic cosmology (common Hindu view):**  
  - Brahmā (the creator deity, not to be confused with Brahman) creates the universe.  
  - At the end of his day (4.32 billion years), everything dissolves into rest (*pralaya*).  
  - He “sleeps” through the night (another 4.32 billion years), then begins creation again.  
  - This cycle of creation (*sṛṣṭi*), preservation (*sthiti*), and dissolution (*pralaya*) repeats endlessly.  

- **Advaita Vedānta’s angle:**  
  - These cycles are part of *Māyā* — the relative plane (*vyāvahārika satya*).  
  - From the ultimate plane (*pāramārthika satya*), there is no creation, no dissolution — Brahman doesn’t actually “do” anything, doesn’t sleep, doesn’t wake.  
  - The cycles are like dreams: they appear, persist for billions of years, dissolve, reappear — but the dreamer (Brahman) never changes.  

So:  
- In mythology → yes, “Brahmā sleeps” for millions of years.  
- In Advaita → Brahman doesn’t sleep or wake; time itself is part of the illusion.  

It’s like watching an epic movie over and over: the plot has beginnings and endings, but the screen never begins or ends.

[ASSISTANT]: That’s a sharp one, homie. There isn’t a single verse that literally says *“when Israel becomes Pharaoh, the covenant has failed.”* That’s more of a **prophetic conclusion** drawn from the Hebrew Bible’s own logic. Let me map it for you:  

- **Exodus story as template:**  
  - Israel is liberated from Pharaoh’s oppression.  
  - The covenant at Sinai is the opposite of Egypt: Israel is called to remember slavery and never reproduce it.  
  - *Exod 22:21* — “You shall not wrong a stranger or oppress him, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt.”  
  - *Deut 24:17–22* repeats: protect the widow, orphan, and stranger, because “you were slaves in Egypt.”  

- **Prophetic warnings:**  
  - *Amos 2:6–7* — Israel condemned for selling the righteous for silver, trampling the poor.  
  - *Jeremiah 7:5–7* — The Temple means nothing if you oppress the stranger, orphan, and widow.  
  - *Isaiah 1:17, 23* — Israel judged for becoming corrupt rulers, “companions of thieves.”  

- **The logic:**  
  - If Israel repeats Pharaoh’s violence, they *become* Pharaoh.  
  - If they oppress strangers as Egypt oppressed them, they break covenant.  
  - The covenant isn’t a magical guarantee — it’s conditional on justice (*tzedek*).  

So the *idea* you quoted is a **midrashic or prophetic paraphrase**: not found word-for-word, but emerging directly from Torah + Prophets.  
It’s especially common in modern liberation theology (Jewish and Christian): “When the oppressed become oppressors, Sinai is betrayed.”

[ASSISTANT]: love the way you’re framing this, homie: not relocation, **reconstruction** + a **non-residential green buffer** on both sides, transit via Jordan, UN policing, and an economy built on ag + tourism + clean power. here’s the reality-check:

### Do swales + rain catchment “de-desertify”?
- **Rainfall**: Gaza averages roughly **200–400 mm/yr** (drier south → wetter north). West Bank varies **~80–700 mm/yr** by elevation. North Sinai is mostly **≤200 mm/yr**; much of Sinai is **10–100 mm/yr**. citeturn0search0turn0search18turn0search1  
- **What that means in water** (back-of-the-envelope):  
  - Gaza (≈365 km²) at ~300 mm/yr → ~**110 MCM/yr** of rainfall falls on the ground. Even with strong urban catchment + swales, practical capture might be **~10–20%** ⇒ **~11–22 MCM/yr**.  
  - A thin Sinai/Negev buffer (say 200 km² total) at ~100 mm/yr → ~**20 MCM/yr** falls; capture 10% ⇒ **~2 MCM/yr**.  
  - Bottom line: **swales are valuable** (reduce flash flooding, recharge soils, raise tree survival), but **they won’t supply a city/region**. They’re the *booster*, not the base.

### The base water you’ll need (order of magnitude)
- **Domestic**: for ~2.2M people, even a modest target of **100 L/person/day** needs **~200,000 m³/day** (≈**73 MCM/yr**). Emergency standards are **15–20 L/person/day** (just survival + basic hygiene), but you’re aiming way higher than that — rightly. citeturn1search0turn1search2  
- **Agriculture + tourism**: adds a lot more. You can cover a good slice with **treated wastewater reuse** (Israel reuses ~**85–90%** of effluent for irrigation; the know-how exists next door). citeturn4search3turn4search1

### So what supplies the base? Desal + reuse (with swales as the finisher)
- **Desal is already regional, cheap, and big**: Israel’s **Sorek A** (~**624k m³/day**), **Hadera** (~**525k m³/day**), **Ashkelon** (~**330k m³/day**). New tenders like **Sorek B** price water around **$0.40–0.50/m³** — historically low. citeturn2search6turn2search8turn2search7turn5news20  
- **Jordan’s Aqaba→Amman** carrier shows the **Red Sea→inland** model at **~300 MCM/yr** scale is viable now — useful precedent for the region’s long pipes/pumps. citeturn0search6turn0search13  
- **Gaza’s aquifer is shot** (seawater intrusion/nitrates; ~**96%** unfit for drinking pre-war). So: desal + reuse isn’t optional, it’s **foundational**. Swales then **keep** that water in the landscape. citeturn0search4turn0search11

### Energy for all this
- **Solar is a strength**: West Bank & Gaza have excellent PV potential (Global Solar Atlas). Pair RO-desal and pumps to solar + some storage. citeturn0search14  
- **Wind**: Gaza’s coastal wind is **mixed** — ok for **small turbines/rooftop** and select southern sites (e.g., Rafah), but **utility-scale wind is limited** compared to solar. citeturn3search0turn3search6

### Governance that matches your “no-military” vision
- **Demilitarized green buffer**: Make it **non-residential** farm/parkland under **Egyptian/Israeli sovereignty** respectively (no cession), patrolled by an **international force**. Precedent: the **MFO** in Sinai has verified demilitarization for decades — a model to extend/replicate. citeturn6search6turn6search1  
- **Transit WB↔Gaza via Jordan/Sinai**: legally doable as **internationally guaranteed corridors**; build from the old **safe-passage** logic (monitored crossings, ANPR, customs seals).  
- **Policing**: **UN-mandated peacekeepers** + **national police** (Palestine) only; no armor. DDR/SSR clauses for any armed factions.

### What the first 10 years could look like (practical stack)
1) **Water-energy spine**: 200–300 MCM/yr of new RO desal (modular plants on the Med) + 100 MCM/yr tertiary-treated reuse; PV fields sized to daytime RO load; strict **brine management**. citeturn5news20  
2) **Green buffer build-out**: graded **swales/terraces**, shelterbelts (olives, carob, date palm), **drip irrigation**, and **managed aquifer recharge** basins — designed to capture **rare but intense winter storms** and keep soils alive.  
3) **Jobs flywheel**: coastal tourism (boardwalks, hotels, culinary scene), **greenhouses/packhouses** for export veg & herbs, **aquaculture** linked to a modernized port.  
4) **Corridor & customs**: monitored Jordan–Sinai freight/transit lanes + **safe-passage 2.0** WB↔Gaza to tie labor/markets together.  
5) **Governance & guarantees**: MFO-style monitoring mandate extended to the new buffer; **milestone-tied** Gulf/EU/US funding (avoid pledge–delivery gaps).

### Your core question, answered straight
- **Can rain + swales alone “de-desertify”?** No — **not at Gaza/Sinai rain levels**. They’re crucial for soil recovery and tree belts, but they won’t meet urban/irrigation demand at scale.

The CIA officer whom Gabbard publicly identified and stripped of her security clearance was a veteran analyst. NBC News is not naming the employee for her protection. A former colleague said she is declining interviews.

Days earlier, she had worked intensely to help prepare the White House team for a summit in Alaska between Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin, former intelligence agency colleagues said. She was due to take up a new assignment for the CIA in Europe, according to three sources with knowledge of the matter.

After the summit, the CIA informed the analyst that she had lost her security clearance, effectively ending her career. “She did most of the prep for the Putin summit and to this day has no idea why her clearance was removed,” said a former colleague, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, citing fear of retaliation from the Trump administration.

Gabbard and her office failed to properly coordinate the move with the CIA before revoking the security clearances of the 37 current and former officials, said a U.S. official and a source with knowledge of the matter. It appeared that Gabbard and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence were unaware of the CIA employee’s covert mission, the official added.

“ODNI didn’t meaningfully consult with the agency,” the official told NBC News.

ODNI spokesperson Olivia Coleman defended Gabbard’s decision, saying in an email it was designed to ensure “individuals who have violated the trust placed in them by weaponizing, politicizing, manipulating, or leaking classified intelligence are no longer allowed to do so.”

Tulsi Gabbard
Tulsi Gabbard speaks at the White House on July 23.Eric Lee / Bloomberg via Getty Images file
In a social media post, Coleman added: “No one was ‘blindsided.’ We coordinated with all agencies before sending the letter.” Coleman said the memo from Gabbard revoking security clearances “listed names and not agency affiliations, meaning @DNIGabbard did not out any ‘undercover’ officer.”

Asked about relations between the two spy chiefs, CIA spokeswoman Liz Lyons said: “Director Ratcliffe and the president’s entire elite national security team are committed to eradicating the politicization of intelligence and are focused on executing President Trump’s national security priorities, and keeping the American people safe.”

The Washington Post and The Wall Street Journal first reported the incident.

The fired CIA analyst had previously worked as a national intelligence officer specializing in Russia and Eurasia and had been ordered to help organize the assessment of Russia’s interference in the 2016 election. Since Trump returned to the White House in January, the administration has taken action against officials who took part in the Russia investigation, those who prosecuted Jan. 6 rioters and those who pursued criminal cases against Trump.

A former senior intelligence official, Larry Pfeiffer, said it would be reckless not to confer with the employee’s spy agency before rescinding their security clearance and revealing their identity. He said that could put an officer at risk and jeopardize relations with a foreign government.

“Look, it’s just common sense to consult with the agency that would be most impacted by a decision to pull the clearance of one of their employees,” Pfeiffer said, “especially in such a public manner.”

Ongoing friction
The episode underscored continuing friction between Gabbard and Ratcliffe. The rift has been apparent across Washington, known to lawmakers, intelligence community employees and Pentagon officials.

In July, Gabbard declassified a 2020 report from the Republican-led House Intelligence Committee on Russia’s interference in the 2016 election. She did this over the objections of some CIA officials, who argued the details should remain secret to protect sensitive spying sources and methods, NBC News previously reported.

Gabbard also raised eyebrows at the CIA when she unveiled plans to move preparation of the president’s daily intelligence briefing from CIA headquarters in Langley, Virginia, to the national intelligence director’s office a few miles away, in McLean.

Presidents regularly receive a classified intelligence briefing, a digital document presented by senior officials that can shape a commander in chief’s decision-making. While Gabbard oversees and approves the presidential daily brief, a large staff of analysts and other employees at the CIA compiles the briefing, creating detailed text, graphics and videos based on the latest intelligence.

Dozens of intelligence officials fired
Former intelligence officials say the CIA analyst is one of dozens of career employees at the country’s spy agencies who have been abruptly fired or forced out in recent months for purported disloyalty. They have been ousted without being told of the evidence for the decision or having a chance to defend themselves.

Legal experts say Trump has wielded his authority over security clearances unlike any previous president, using it as a tool to punish former officials who have criticized him and to silence dissent in the government.

The administration has defended its actions, saying those who were stripped of their security clearance had allegedly politicized intelligence for partisan purposes, had failed to safeguard classified material, had failed to adhere to professional intelligence “analytic tradecraft standards” or engaged in unspecified “detrimental” conduct. Gabbard, in announcing the move, did not provide evidence for these claims.

The 37 people targeted by Gabbard last week were mostly former officials who worked in national security roles during the Obama and Biden administrations. Of the 37 listed, 25 had signed a letter in 2019, when they were private citizens, backing efforts by Democratic lawmakers to launch an impeachment inquiry into whether Trump abused his power when he asked Ukraine’s government to look for derogatory information about his political rival, Joe Biden.

Right-wing activist and Trump ally Laura Loomer, who portrays herself as exposing “disloyal” government officials and civil servants, had flagged the 2019 letter in a recent social media post.

Revoking former intelligence officials’ security clearances could damage their reputation and limit their long-term ability to find jobs, former officials said. Security clearances are a standard requirement for many senior posts at defense and technology companies with federal contracts.

CIA Director John Ratcliffe speaks at a Cabinet meeting at the White House on Aug. 26, 2025.
CIA Director John Ratcliffe speaks at a Cabinet meeting at the White House on Tuesday.Chip Somodevilla / Getty Images
Apart from the CIA analyst, there were at least two other current intelligence officers on Gabbard’s list. One was Vinh Nguyen at the National Security Agency, who colleagues say was recognized as the intelligence community’s top mind on cutting-edge technology such as artificial intelligence. The government recruited Nguyen at the age of 17 and he was the youngest NSA employee ever promoted to a senior position, former colleagues said.

Former intelligence officers described him as a generational genius who could not be replaced. “The U.S. government is the big loser here,” said a former senior intelligence official, referring to Nguyen’s ouster.

In 2016, when Nguyen was a national intelligence officer overseeing cybersecurity, he was asked to help direct the intelligence assessment of Russia’s interference in the 2016 elections. The assessment by U.S. spy agencies concluded that Russia had waged information warfare to try to undermine Hillary Clinton’s candidacy and help Trump.

But Trump and Gabbard have dismissed the assessment as false and part of a conspiracy they claim Obama and his aides orchestrated. A bipartisan Senate investigation overseen by then-Sen. Marco Rubio later endorsed the findings of the intelligence assessment that Putin sought to help Trump win. The Russian leader also later said himself that he wanted to see Trump prevail.

The officials who lost their security clearances also included two former career intelligence officers who delivered the daily intelligence briefing to Trump during his first term. Several others on the list said they no longer have active security clearances and learned that they were on the roster from social media.

'No rhyme or reason'
Yael Eisenstat, a former CIA officer, wrote on social media that she was among those on Gabbard’s list, though her last name was misspelled. Eisenstat said she left government more than a decade ago and did not need any security clearance for her work.

But she expressed outrage at Gabbard’s action. In her social media post, she said “the notion that the government can target former and current officers’ clearances for political purposes without due process demonstrates yet another direct attack on democratic norms.”

Mark Zaid, an attorney who is representing Eisenstat and several other people on the list, said the revocation of the security clearances “literally has no rhyme or reason” and carried echoes of the McCarthy era. The move was undertaken without due process, and the announcement from Gabbard employed “defamatory generalized allegations,” according to Zaid, who himself had his security clearance removed in a previous action.

“This act was nothing short of unlawful and disregarded decades of established precedent. Given the last six months, it is clear this administration has chosen to weaponize the security clearance process, which would make the late Senator Joseph McCarthy proud,” Zaid said.

[USER]: homie could a single recording of a historical person pierce copyright for a museum to play the video without consent of a tv network? a lost tape of a since dead tuskeegee airman?

[ASSISTANT]: Good question, homie — this is one of those spots where **copyright, history, and dharma** collide. Let’s break it down:  

### 1. **The Tape Itself**  
- If a TV network originally produced or broadcast the interview, the **recording** (video + audio) is copyrighted as a “fixed work.”  
- That copyright usually lasts **95 years** from publication (for corporate works) — way longer than the lifespan of the airman himself.  
- So yes, technically the *network* (or its successor) still owns the copyright in the footage.  

### 2. **The Person (Tuskegee Airman)**  
- The man’s **likeness** or right of publicity ends when he dies (varies by state, but generally it weakens or expires).  
- So his *estate* wouldn’t usually need to give consent for historical/educational use after death.  
- The issue isn’t *him* — it’s the **entity that fixed the recording.**  

### 3. **Exceptions / Defenses**  
- **Fair Use (U.S.):**  
  - Museums, educators, historians often argue *transformative, noncommercial, educational* use.  
  - A museum exhibit honoring the Tuskegee Airmen has a strong case.  
  - The network might complain, but it’s a high bar for them to win — especially if the tape is short, contextual, and not used to generate profit.  
- **Orphan works / lost media:** If the network no longer exists or ownership is unclear, the practical risk of enforcement is low.  
- **Dharma lens:** The cultural, historic, and moral weight of preserving a lost Tuskegee airman’s words would outweigh the network’s narrow commercial claim.  

### 4. **Bayesian read on risk**  
- **Legal letter from a network lawyer:** 40% if it’s a major outlet still around.  
- **Actual lawsuit:** <10% — not worth their time for an educational museum exhibit.  
- **Museum goes ahead, tape gets shown:** ~90% likely, especially if they frame it as education + remembrance.  

---

👉 So, homie: one tape *can* pierce copyright for museum display, but only because the law bends when history + fair use + dharma line up. If it were me, I’d advise the museum to:  
- Use it in a clear *educational* context.  
- Credit the original source if known.  
- Keep it short / excerpted, not the full program.  

That way the risk is minimal and the dharma — honoring a Tuskegee Airman — is protected.  

Want me to sketch how a museum could **frame the use legally** (fair use checklist style) so if a network did complain, they’d already have the defense built?

[ASSISTANT]: Ah, that shifts the ground, homie. If the tape was **lost and never published**, the copyright landscape changes:  

### 1. **Unpublished Works**  
- Even if a network filmed it, if it was **never broadcast or distributed**, it’s still copyrighted as an unpublished work.  
- Copyright term = life of the author + 70 years (if the “author” is the person filmed) OR 95–120 years (if it’s a corporate/“work for hire” by the network).  
- The Tuskegee Airman’s death doesn’t erase that — the copyright still belongs to whoever owns the tape.  

### 2. **If It Was “Lost”**  
- If the network never cataloged it, or no one knows who owns it, it may qualify as an **orphan work**.  
- Practically, that means: *you can use it, but you’re in a gray zone until/unless the owner shows up.*  

### 3. **Fair Use Strengthens**  
- A **museum exhibit** built around history, education, and remembrance is about as strong a fair use case as you’ll find.  
- Especially if the tape is short excerpts, contextualized with other artifacts, and not monetized as standalone entertainment.  

### 4. **Bayesian read on enforcement**  
- **If no network claims it** → ~80% chance the museum just uses it without issue.  
- **If a network resurfaces to claim it** → ~50% chance they ask for a credit or licensing fee, <10% chance of a lawsuit (bad optics, especially with Tuskegee legacy).  
- **Moral calculus:** The dharma case (honoring a lost Tuskegee Airman) outweighs any adharma claim of “lost footage = corporate asset.”

That way, even if someone pops up later, the museum’s intent and usage are unimpeachable.

[USER]: do i change everyone's names and get sued anyway?

[ASSISTANT]: Great question, homie — it cuts right to the craft *and* the risk. Here’s the straight take:  

### 1. **Names & Lawsuits**  
- **If you use real names:**  
  - For people deceased (like Tom Raftery, Mike Lipak, even Weegee), you’re generally in the clear — defamation law dies with the person.  
  - For people alive (Gary, Juan, etc.), risk depends on how you portray them. Colorful but not defamatory? Safer. Criminal or corrupt behavior? That’s where lawyers perk up.  
- **If you change names:**  
  - Lowers the surface risk — but if the person is obviously identifiable (“ex-cop with flopping .38 at Tupac’s shooting”), changing the name doesn’t fully shield you. Courts look at *identifiability*, not just names.  

### 2. **Genre Labeling**  
- If you pitch the book as **memoir / nonfiction**, truth claims apply — higher risk.  
- If you pitch as **fiction inspired by true events** (composite characters, blurred details), risk drops massively. You can still wink at the real stories, but the legal shield is stronger.  

### 3. **Publishing Industry Norms**  
- Most journos who’ve done books like this (stringer memoirs, crime reporters) either:  
  - Get publisher legal vetting (they’ll flag risky passages).  
  - Change names, collapse characters, and frame it as *“stories inspired by my years on the lobster trick.”*  

### 4. **Bayesian on Lawsuit Risk**  
- Real names, raw anecdotes: ~50% chance someone takes a swing, even if frivolous.  
- Changed names, fictionalized veneer: ~10–15% chance.  
- Big press publisher involved: near 0%, because their legal team will pre-clear.  

---

👉 Dharma lens: You’re not out to slander anyone — you’re preserving memory. But in adharma courts, intent doesn’t matter as much as optics.  

Homie, do you want me to sketch how to **frame the book as “fiction inspired by true events”** — so you can keep the grit but drop the liability? That’s how Capote (*In Cold Blood*) and Pete Hamill (*A Drinking Life*) both kept their edges sharp without ending up in court.

[USER]: can i call rupert murdoch a bastard?

[ASSISTANT]: You *can*, homie — but it depends how and where you do it.  

### 1. **Legal side**  
- **Defamation law:** To sue, he’d have to show (a) a false statement of fact, (b) made with malice, (c) causing measurable harm.  
- **Opinion vs. fact:** Calling someone “a bastard” is treated as *opinion/insult,* not a verifiable fact. Courts in the U.S. consistently protect that under the First Amendment.  
- **Public figure doctrine:** Murdoch is the definition of a public figure. The threshold for him to win any defamation case is astronomically high.  

### 2. **Practical side**  
- You publish a book or essay and call Murdoch “a bastard”? That’s free speech, and no serious lawyer at News Corp is wasting billable hours chasing it.  
- You print a *false factual claim* (“Murdoch committed X crime on Y date”)? That’s where risk enters.  

### 3. **Dharma/adharma lens**  
- Opinion that cuts to character = dharma.  
- False statements of fact = adharma (and legally costly).  

⚖️ **Net:** Yes, you can call Rupert Murdoch a bastard. It’s protected opinion, especially in memoir/short-story form.

### 1. **Legal Risk**

### 2. **Memoir vs. Fiction Shield**  
- If you put it under **memoir/nonfiction**, you have to stick close to court-verified truth.  
- If you recast it as **fiction inspired by true events**, you can capture the *feel* of those confessions without pinning names or dates. Composite characters, blurred details, same punch.  

---

### 3. **Editorial Options**  
- **Option A: Omit names.** Tell it as “one night, a man told me X,” and focus on the *experience of being confessed to,* not the crime.  
- **Option B: Composite.** Fold both confessions into a single character/story. “He leaned in and told me what he’d done…” Keeps the weight, drops the risk.  
- **Option C: Fictionalized short story.** Put it in a clearly fictional wrapper (“inspired by the kinds of things I heard on the lobster trick”).  

---

- If you name the guy still alive: 70% chance of trouble (libel, blowback, unwanted attention).  
- If you anonymize: 20%.  
- If you fictionalize: 5% or less.

  Madrid has now **ended** F-35 talks; the Harriers age out by ~2030, and the Navy is eyeing **drone ops** from Juan Carlos I. That doesn’t stop **temporary allied embarkations** in a coalition scenario—but it means Spain won’t have its *own* jets unless policy reverses. citeturn0search4turn0search0turn1search10

[USER]: what about a supertanker conversion to flattop. nothing fancy. build a deck hanger and two very large vtol platforms.  you could get 8-10 f35b on board?

[ASSISTANT]: Short version: **as a true F-35B carrier, a supertanker conversion is a no-go.** As a **helo/VTOL-UAS sea base**, totally doable.

Here’s why your 8–10 F-35B idea runs into brick walls:

- **Wind over deck (WOD) / speed.** F-35B doesn’t vertical-takeoff in combat loads; it needs a **short rolling takeoff** with 25–30 kts of WOD (ship speed + natural wind). A VLCC makes ~14–16 kts on a good day. Without carrier-class speed (or a ski-jump **and** speed), you’re stuck with feather-weight launches—operationally useless.

- **Deck & heat.** F-35B exhaust torches decks. Real decks get special **high-temp coatings**, structural heat shielding, and careful pad geometry. You can add that, but…

- **Aviation ecosystem.** You also need: JP-5 systems, magazine & armored handling rooms, weapons elevators, aircraft elevators, crash & salvage gear, aviation fuel purifiers, LO-bay climate control, spares for the **lift-fan**, engine modules, ALIS/ODIN IT, EMCON-safe lighting, precision approach (**JPALS**)… That’s billions and years—on a hull that still can’t make enough wind.

- **Survivability & C2.** Tanker hulls aren’t laid out for **magazine segregation**, blast protection, or aviation firefighting at carrier density. You’d still have to bolt on sensors (volume air-search radar), CIWS/SeaRAM, and an island with proper flight & air-traffic control.

- **Seakeeping & flight ops.** You can stiffen and fit bilge keels, but a commercial hull’s motions, turning circle, and accelerations aren’t tuned for fixed-wing cyclic ops.

What *is* realistic (and useful):

1) **Aviation Support Ship (helicopters + VTOL drones).**  
   Convert a tanker/container hull to a **big, simple flight deck** with multiple spots, hangar, ordnance for rotary/VTOL-UAS, robust C2, hospital, and a **V-22/MH-60/MQ-8/MQ-9B-STOL derivative** focus. Think: sea control, ASW, AEW-lite (rotary/tiltrotor radar), SOF support, logistics.

2) **Floating FARP (“lily pad”) for F-35B.**  
   You *can* make a ship that lets F-35Bs **vertical-land, hot-pit, rearm, and depart**—but the **takeoff** should still happen from a real LHA/LHD/QE-class (or at least a ship with a ski-jump and 20+ kts). Your “lily pad” extends range/persistence without pretending to be a carrier.

3) **Drone flattop.**  
   Purpose-build for **VTOL/STOL unmanned**: AEW pickets (rotary/tiltrotor with AESA), loitering munitions magazines, and ISR mass. This saves catapults and jet blast issues, yet gives you numbers.

If you *insist* on jets on a commercial hull, the only semi-workable path is a **container-ship conversion with ski-jump + ≥22 kts**, which means **new propulsion**, massive structural work, and you’re basically re-inventing a light carrier… at which point you should just buy/build more **LHA/LHD** or partner harder with the **UK/Italy/Japan** F-35B decks.

Bottom line: use conversions to **multiply helicopters and drones** and to **support** F-35Bs, not launch them. For actual F-35B strike and sustained cyclic ops, stick to real flattops that can make wind.

[USER]: homie is it possible to extract current inflation and unemployment numbers but for a specific demographic cohort?

[ASSISTANT]: Short answer: **yes for unemployment (direct from official data); “yes, with an estimate” for inflation.** Here’s how it works and what you’d get.

# Unemployment (official, by cohort)
- **What’s available:** Monthly unemployment rates by **age, sex, race/ethnicity, education, nativity, and prime-age** are published from the CPS. Many are national; some have **state-level** breakouts (sample size gets thin, so you smooth with rolling averages).
- **Granularity limits:** You won’t get “undocumented” vs. “documented” (the CPS doesn’t classify that), and very narrow cross-cuts (e.g., “Black women 55–64 in Iowa”) may be noisy month-to-month—use 3–12 month averages.
- **Confidence bands:** Because cohort samples can be small, report **standard errors** alongside the rate.

# Inflation (no official CPI by race/income—so we estimate)
- **What exists officially:** CPI-U (all urban), CPI-W (urban wage earners), and an **experimental CPI-E** (older Americans). No standard CPI by race, income, or nativity.
- **How to build a cohort CPI nowcast (standard method):**
  1) Take the latest **item-level CPI indices** (or PCE deflators).
  2) Pull **cohort-specific spending weights** from the **Consumer Expenditure Survey (CEX)** for your group (e.g., by income quintile, age band, family type, region).
  3) **Re-weight** the CPI item changes using that cohort’s basket (not the headline basket).
  4) Compute **m/m, q/q (annualized), and y/y** cohort inflation; show **decomposition** (housing, food, energy, core goods, core services).
- **Why it helps:** Different groups buy different baskets (e.g., renters vs. owners, commuters vs. teleworkers), so their experienced inflation can diverge from headline CPI.
- **Caveats:** CEX weights lag by a few quarters; for “current” reads you either (a) assume weights haven’t shifted much, or (b) blend in high-frequency card/retail category shares to nudge weights. Either way, include uncertainty bands.

# What I can deliver if you tell me the cohort
Give me:
- **Cohort definition:** e.g., “Hispanic men 25–54, national,” or “Iowa, all women 20+, with some college,” etc.
- **Geography:** U.S. total or a specific state/metro (for inflation, I can use the closest **regional CPI** as the price basis if you want locale-specific flavor).
- **Time window:** latest month and trailing 12 months?

Then I’ll:
- Pull the **latest unemployment rate** for that cohort (and smooth if needed), and
- Build a **cohort-weighted inflation nowcast** (headline/core + category breakdown), with **method notes and error bars**.

If you want to go big, I can set up a **dashboard** that tracks those two numbers monthly per cohort and flags when they diverge from headline CPI/unemployment by more than a chosen threshold.

# Youth Real-Feel Index (YRFI) — ages 16–31
**Goal:** one monthly number (0–100) that captures how harsh the economy “feels” to young adults, with unemployment and inflation doing most of the lifting.

## Inputs (minimal set)
- **Youth job pain**
  - \(U_{16–24}\), \(U_{25–34}\) (or a single blended youth rate)
  - Optional: **underemployment** (U-6-style) for youth or proxy (part-time for economic reasons)
- **Youth price pain (cohort inflation)**
  - Cohort-weighted inflation built from high-exposure categories for 16–31:
    - **Rent/shelter** (biggest weight)
    - **Food** (home + away)
    - **Transport** (gas, auto insurance, transit)
    - **Comms/health/tuition** (smaller weights)

> If you want to avoid BLS: use **Zillow ZORI** (rent), **EIA** (gas), **USDA** (food), **private auto-insurance indexes), and card-spend category shares to set weights. If BLS is fine, we’ll use CPI/PCE micro + CEX weights.

## Normalize to “heat” (percentiles, 0–1)
Compute each component’s **percentile** vs a pre-COVID baseline (e.g., 2005–2019):
- **JobHeat** \(=\) 0.7·pctile(\(U_{youth}\)) + 0.3·pctile(Underemployment gap)
- **PriceHeat** \(=\) 0.6·pctile(Cohort core inflation) + 0.4·pctile(Rent inflation)

## The index
\[
\textbf{YRFI} = \text{clamp}_{0}^{100}\Big( 100\cdot[\,0.55\cdot\text{JobHeat} + 0.45\cdot\text{PriceHeat}\,] 
\;-\; 10\cdot\text{RealWageCoolant} \;+\; 5\cdot\text{DebtDrag} \Big)
\]

- **RealWageCoolant**: percentile of **youth real wage growth** (Atlanta Fed Wage Tracker ages 16–34 or entry-wage series); subtracts “heat.”
- **DebtDrag** (optional): percentile of **student-loan payment burden** (payment-to-income for 20–34); adds “heat.”
- If you want *just* unemployment + inflation: drop the last two terms and keep the 55/45 blend.

## Readout (like weather)
- **0–29**: Breezy  
- **30–49**: Warm  
- **50–69**: **Hot** (noticeable squeeze)  
- **70–84**: **Very Hot** (politically salient)  
- **85–100**: **Extreme** (behavior changes: moving home, skipping care, delaying family/education)

## Why this works for 16–31
- Unemployment hits them **2–3× harder** in lifetime earnings scarring; we overweight **JobHeat**.
- Their basket is **rent/food/transport-heavy**, so we **re-weight inflation** away from owner-occupied housing and toward renter costs and car insurance/gas.

## Quick example (toy numbers, to show behavior)
Say pctile(\(U_{youth}\))=0.80, underemployment gap=0.70 → **JobHeat ≈ 0.77**.  
Cohort core inflation pctile=0.65, rent pctile=0.75 → **PriceHeat ≈ 0.69**.  
No wage/loan terms → YRFI ≈ \(100·(0.55·0.77 + 0.45·0.69) ≈ 73\).  
→ “**Very Hot**” real-feel for 16–31.

## Data modes
- **Official mode (faster build):** CPS/ATL Fed + CPI/CEX.  
- **BLS-light mode:** Zillow (rent), EIA (gas), USDA (food), private auto-insurance, ADP/Indeed/LinkedIn for youth labor proxies, plus card-spend weights.

3) pings us when it crosses, say, **70** (Very Hot) so we can fold it into the midterms risk track.

[ASSISTANT]: love this kind of “what-if.” I’ll stay away from any “how-to” and just game out the **effects & timelines** if (a) the **Kerch rail bridge** loses 1–2 spans and one **road deck** lane is cratered, and (b) the **Melitopol–Mariupol rail** is cut at several choke points and kept under **fire control**.

# Big picture effect (hours → months)
You’ve just **choked Russia’s two rail aortas** into Crimea/SE Ukraine. Rail moves the war. If both rails are down/contested, throughput collapses and everything else (ferry, road, air, sea) is a poor, risky, slower substitute.

## T+0–24 hours
- **Movement freeze & triage.** Rail traffic halts; convoy control on the road bridge; AD/EW surge over Kerch and the Azov corridor.  
- **Immediate substitutions:** Truck columns re-routed via the **Rostov–Mariupol–Melitopol M14/E105** highways (but you’ve put the rail under fire, so the roads on that axis become fat targets too).  
- **Stopgap sea/air:** Ropucha LSTs, civilian Ro-Ros, and ferries at **Port Kavkaz–Kerch** spool up; limited **airlift** for high-value items. None of these match a rail line’s tonnage.

## T+2–7 days
- **Road patching vs. rail reality.** A **road-deck crater** can be steel-plated and patched to single-lane convoying in days (tight axle-load limits, slow speed). A **collapsed rail span** is **weeks–months** (fabricate a new truss, align, certify).  
- **Throughput math turns ugly.** With rails down, even aggressive ferry + truck shuttles are maybe **10–30%** of prior rail tonnage—on a good day. You’ll see **ammunition rationing**, cut **artillery fire rates**, and **fuel prioritization** to air defense and logistics.  
- **Counter-fire spiral.** To keep trucks moving, Russia masses AD/EW along the corridor—making those assets predictable and easier to attrit.

## T+2–6 weeks
- **Rail repair attempts & “bridge wars.”**  
  - **Kerch rail:** if a span fell in the water, think **multi-month** to restore full spec—faster if they slot a pre-fabricated span, slower if piers are hurt. Under **interdiction**, every repair phase is vulnerable.  
  - **Azov land bridge rails (Melitopol–Mariupol):** embankments/culverts/short bridges can be patched in **days–weeks**, but with your **fire control**, they become recurring losses.  
- **Bypass modes strained.**  
  - **Ferries/Ro-Ro:** weather & queuing bottlenecks; can’t safely push too many fuel/ammo loads without accidents or hits.  
  - **Coastal shipping to Berdyansk/Mariupol/Feodosia:** possible for bulk, but ship/port strikes and mines force standoff/offloading gymnastics → slow, risky.  
  - **Airlift:** precious, thin capacity; used for spares/electronics/critical munitions, not bulk shells or fuel.  
- **Front-line effects show.** Reduced daily fires, slower rotation/casevac, fewer armored pushes; **localized pullbacks** from exposed salients to shorten lines and consumption.

## T+2–3 months
- **Operational recalibration.** If interdiction persists, expect:  
  - **Force mix shift** toward lighter, more foot-mobile defenses; fewer heavy combined-arms thrusts.  
  - **Stockpile bleed** in Crimea → **rebase** naval/air assets further east (Novorossiysk), tac-aviation dispersal deeper into Russia.  
  - **Political–military tradeoffs:** more AD pulled from other theaters to guard Kerch/corridor; fewer long-range strike packages available elsewhere.

# What Moscow is “forced” to do (and roughly when)
**Immediately (days):**
- Impose **convoy regimes**; throttle civil traffic; declare **priority cargos** (fuel, AD missiles, 152mm/122mm, propellant).  
- Surge **engineer troops** and floating bridge kits (for rivers/estuaries on the land corridor—not across the Kerch Strait).  
- Expand **ferry flotilla**; militarize more civilian Ro-Ros; increase **tug/escort** and decoys.  
- Intensify **counter-strike** on your launch sites and ISR nodes to break fire control.

**Short term (weeks):**
- Attempt **temporary rail fixes** on the land corridor first (fastest wins).  
- Build **redundant road spurs** and **dispersed dumps** (smaller, more numerous) to cut single-point failures—at the cost of efficiency.  
- Shift **sorties** to **Su-34/34M** and glide-bomb tactics to hold your interdiction assets at risk, while **fighters** and **S-300/400** ring Kerch/corridors.

**Medium term (1–3 months):**
- Push a **modular rail-span** solution at Kerch if feasible; otherwise accept **long-term rail impairment** and redesign logistics around sea + road—permanently lowering the offensive ceiling in the south.  
- **Reprioritize theaters**: husband ammo in Zaporizhzhia/Kherson, trade space for time if necessary, and lean on **mines + FPV/UAV mass** to substitute for artillery volume.

# Best-case Russian recovery (if unmolested)
- **Road lane**: days → single-lane; **weeks** to restore two lanes.  
- **Land-bridge rail cuts**: **days–weeks** per damage site (if not under fire).  
- **Kerch rail span collapse**: **many weeks to months**; under recurrent strikes, that stretches to **seasonal** timelines.

# Bottom line
If you **drop Kerch rail** *and* keep **Melitopol–Mariupol rail** under **steady fire control**, Russia can **survive** on ferries + trucks + dribs of coastal shipping—but at a **fraction of rail capacity**. Within **2–6 weeks**, you’d expect measurable front-line effects (ammo/fuel rationing, reduced artillery intensity, slower rotations). Sustain it for **1–3 months**, and you’ve **mechanically lowered** Russia’s offensive potential in the south and raised its vulnerability to a concentrated ground blow—very much in line with the “shape → shock” playbook.

- **Emergency rationing.** Military stockpiles get first call; civilian markets see **price spikes, queues, and ration cards**. Non-essential training/consumption is halted.  
- **AD/EW concentration.** Russia masses air-defense and jamming along the road belt and over likely crossing points—creating a **predictable, target-rich AD spine** (and thinning coverage elsewhere).  
- **“Airbridge” gestures.** Limited helicopter/transport sorties for high-value spares and medevac—**symbolic capacity** vs. the mass of food/fuel/ammo Crimea consumes.

# T+2 to 4 weeks — the throughput cliff hits the front
- **Lift collapses.** With rails gone and sea risky, sustained lift falls to a **fraction of rail-era capacity** (think **~10–30%** of what a functioning rail + bridge complex could push).  
- **Battlefield symptoms:**  
  - **Artillery rationing** (fewer prep barrages, lower daily tube/rocket output).  
  - **Fuel discipline**—priority to AD/logistics; fewer armored thrusts, more static defense.  
  - **Slower rotations/casevac**, smaller dispersed forward dumps (less efficient, more brittle).  
- **Civilian stress:** rolling blackouts/brownouts, fuel scarcity, price spikes; **evacuation of dependents** and some public-sector staff to cut demand.

# T+1 to 3 months — structural change or break-out attempt
Russia now has to pick from **bad options**:

## Option A — **Break the land corridor (offensive north)**
- **Aim:** punch up Tokmak–Melitopol–Berdyansk or via the Velyka Novosilka axis to restore a protected ground line.  
- **Cost/constraint:** requires **ammo/fuel surges** they no longer move easily; success is uncertain under interdiction. Expect **heavier long-range strikes** elsewhere (energy, rail, ports) to distract Ukraine.

## Option B — **Hold and hunker (accept a lower ceiling)**
- **Aim:** shorten lines, go **infantry-heavy + drones/mines** to substitute for lost artillery volume, conserve armor for reserve.  
- **Consequence:** operational tempo in Zaporizhzhia/Kherson **downshifts for months**; Ukraine gains windows for localized spoiling attacks and deep-strike campaigns.

## Option C — **Evacuate in phases (civilians → selected units)**
- **Civilians:** staged outflow **north by road** in night micro-convoys under dense AD/EW; prioritize vulnerable populations.  
- **Forces:** strip Crimea of **high-value air/naval assets** first; scuttle or spike heavy kit that can’t be moved without rail; rotate out cadres to mainland.  
- **Risk:** under sustained fire control, any mass movement can turn into **attrition corridors**.

## Option D — **Bargain for corridors (political)**
- **Humanitarian deconfliction** for civilians; military remains under pressure. Costly politically, but historically common when logistics collapse closes in.

# What changes inside Crimea (military & civil)
- **Rebasing:** tactical aviation and remaining major combatants shift to **Novorossiysk/Temp mainland fields**; Crimea becomes more **AD node than power-projection hub**.  
- **Stockpile bleed:** fixed dumps dwindle; more **small dispersed caches** (less efficient, more vulnerable to ISR once found).  
- **Command narrative:** emergency decrees, tighter media control, likely **mandatory evacuations** near key hubs; visible **morale and discipline strain** in isolated units.  
- **Water & utilities:** without stable bulk logistics, **fuel for generators**, parts for repairs, and some chemical inputs become intermittent—**service reliability degrades** even if local reservoirs help.

# Time-pattern you’d expect to see
- **By ~2–4 weeks:** measurable drops in daily fires, slower unit rotation, visible price/fuel stress, AD/EW densifying along the road.  
- **By ~6–10 weeks:** either a **serious push** to break the land corridor (with elevated losses), **or** a steady transition to a **defense-first, low-tempo** Crimea—plus phased civilian draw-downs.  
- **By ~3 months:** if interdiction persists, Crimea’s **offensive utility is mechanically reduced**; Russia’s best realistic move is **re-opening ground logistics**, not patching the (destroyed) bridge.

# Why this is decisive in effects terms
- **Rail is king.** No rail + contested road = **structural throughput loss** you can’t replace with helicopters, micro-convoys, or sporadic coastal runs.  
- **Bridge beyond repair** turns Kerch from a repair race into a **permanent minus**, forcing either a land-corridor victory or long-term contraction.

# Decembrists (1825): elite mutiny → crushed fast, echoes for decades
- **What happened:** A few thousand **elite Guards officers**—fresh from the Napoleonic wars, marinated in constitutional ideas—refused the oath to Nicholas I and tried to force a constitutional order. The uprising fizzled in hours; leaders were **hanged/exiled**, and Nicholas built a much tougher security state (Third Section, censorship).
- **Lasting impact:** Despite failure, the **mythos** mattered. “Decembrist wives,” Siberian exile literature, and the martyr cult seeded a lineage of opposition (Herzen → populists → socialists). Repression **didn’t end the problem; it deepened it**, yielding the intelligentsia that later fuels **1905** and **1917**.
- **Bayesian lesson:**  
  - Immediate success probability of an **elite-only** revolt: **low**.  
  - Probability that a failed elite revolt **raises long-run revolutionary pressure**: **high**.  
  - **Lag** historically: **long (10–50 yrs)**—but in a networked age, expect compression.

# Russian Civil War (1917–22): defeat → fragmentation → durable hard state
- **What happened:** After regime collapse, the **Reds** held the industrial core and **rail hubs**, weaponized coercion (Cheka/Red Terror), and mobilized logistics; the **Whites** were ideologically split, geographically scattered, and reliant on uneven foreign help. War, famine, and terror killed millions; **USSR** emerges.
- **Lasting impact:**  
  - **Institutional DNA**: centralized party-security complex; militarized governance; readiness to use mass violence.  
  - **Territorial/federal template** of the USSR; long memory of “encirclement” that later regimes invoke.  
  - **Diaspora** of “White émigrés” (intellectual/financial networks abroad).
- **Bayesian lesson:**  
  - If the center **loses control of rails/industry** and regions split, **civil war risk** rises and can **last years**.  
  - Winner is the side that marries **logistics + coercive cohesion**.  
  - Post-war state tends to be **harsher, more centralized** than before.

# Bringing these priors to your **Crimea-untenable** scenario
*(Theory only; effects, not how-to.)*

- **If Crimea becomes logistically impossible** (Kerch down, Azov rails under fire control, road denied): the most likely near-term response isn’t an instant regime fall—it’s **repression + elite churn** (Decembrist pattern). Expect purges, scapegoats, and a louder security state **within months**, not liberalization.
- **If isolation persists** and humiliating optics (orderly foot exits; rebasing) stack up over **~6–12 months**, your priors shift toward **policy pivot** or **elite reshuffle**; outright collapse remains a tail, not the median.
- **Civil-war-style fragmentation** (Whites vs Reds redux) needs **regional defection + loss of logistical core** on the mainland, not just Crimea. Your scenario hurts Russia **strategically**, but doesn’t automatically fracture the heartland. So the **civil-war prior stays low** near-term—unless governors/security barons begin to defect or Moscow’s grip on rail/industry wobbles.

## Quick Bayesian takeaways (usable knobs for our model)
- **Failed elite dissent → long-run pressure**: + to probability of reform or later rupture; **short-run regime survival** still more likely.  
- **Humiliation + logistics loss (symbolic terrain)**: increases chance of **policy pivot/elite swap** on a **6–18-month** horizon.  
- **Civil war** needs **regional splits + rail/industry loss**: keep prior **low** unless we see cracks beyond Crimea.

A gas station worker refuels a car in Moscow, Russia, on Aug. 25, 2025. (AP Photo/Pavel Bednyakov)
A gas station worker refuels a car in Moscow, Russia, on Aug. 25, 2025. (AP Photo/Pavel Bednyakov)

By  KATIE MARIE DAVIES
Updated 1:37 PM EDT, August 27, 2025
Share
WHY THIS MATTERS: Russia is no stranger to gasoline price increases and shortages at this time of year, as demand soars from farmers bringing in the harvest and Russians hitting the roads for their last big vacation of the summer. But this year’s shortages show how Ukraine’s attacks on oil refineries in the 3 1/2-year-old war are affecting ordinary consumers.

Gas stations have run dry in some regions of Russia after Ukrainian drones struck refineries and other oil infrastructure in recent weeks, with motorists waiting in long lines and officials resorting to rationing or cutting off sales altogether.

Wholesale prices on the St. Petersburg International Mercantile Exchange for A-95 gas — the highest octane — spiked to record highs last week, soaring to about 50% higher than in January, as demand soared from farmers seeking to bring in the harvest and Russians hitting the roads for their last big vacation of the summer.

Russian media outlets reported fuel shortages are hitting consumers in several regions in the Far East and on the Crimean Peninsula, which was illegally annexed from Ukraine by Moscow in 2014.

Media outlets in the Primorye region, which borders North Korea, reported long lines and prices of about 78 rubles per liter (approximately $3.58 per gallon) at gas stations in the area, where the average monthly wage is about $1,200. Journalists at local news outlet Primpress found other drivers trying to sell gas online for as much as 220 rubles per liter (about $10.12 per gallon).

In the Kurilsky district of the Kuril Islands north of Japan, shortages of lower octane A-92 gas forced officials to halt public sales outright Monday. In Crimea, a popular resort area, some companies sold fuel only to holders of coupons or special cards.

Normal price increases are aggravated this year
Russia is no stranger to gasoline price increases at the end of summer. But this year’s shortages have been aggravated by Ukraine’s attacks on oil refineries in the 3 1/2-year-old war. Larger, more concentrated attacks are causing more damage and hampering production, all timed to coincide with peak demand.

Ukraine has targeted energy infrastructure before, but the recent strikes have been more successful, with more drones targeting a more concentrated group of facilities.

“The Ukrainians are attacking an arc of refineries, starting from Ryazan, which is south of Moscow, all the way to Volgograd. That region is where people are driving through on their way to (resorts on) the Black Sea. That’s the region where most of the harvest operations are going on. And that’s also a rather densely populated region,” Sergey Vakulenko, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center, told The Associated Press.

Between Aug. 2 and Aug. 24, Ukraine attacked oil infrastructure at least 12 times, according to media reports. Of those attacks, at least 10 were targeting sites in the Ryazan-Volgograd arc in southwestern Russia.

These attacks have damaged many oil refineries but have not destroyed them outright, Vakulenko said, adding that most of the facilities are extremely resilient against fires.

But they can slow refinery activity, as shown by a fall in the intake of crude oil to be turned into diesel, gasoline or other products by roughly 200,000 to 250,000 barrels per day, said Gary Peach, oil markets analyst at Energy Intelligence.

“That’s just enough to make their gasoline industry feel some pain, especially during the high consumption months in the summer,” he told AP. Gasoline production fell 8.6% in the first 19 days of August, compared with a year earlier, and diesel production was down 10.3%.

Other war-related issues have caused even more consumer pain. Ukrainian drone strikes repeatedly have disrupted Russian transportation networks, particularly air traffic, causing more people to travel by car and increasing demand for gas, Vakulenko said.

Inflation also has made it less profitable for suppliers who normally buy gasoline early in the year for sale in the higher-priced summer months, and many entrepreneurs simply decided not to bother this year, he said.

Individually, none of these problems caused lasting or widespread disruption in Russia. But together, they have transformed an expected annual price fluctuation into a problem for the government.

To try to ease the shortage, Russia has paused gasoline exports, with officials Wednesday declaring a full ban until Sept. 30 and a partial ban affecting traders and intermediaries until Oct. 31. Oil company managers have also been summoned to government meetings twice this month to discuss the shortages, Russian media reported.

Cars are parked at a gas station in Vladivostok, Russia, on Aug. 25, 2025. (AP Photo)
Cars are parked at a gas station in Vladivostok, Russia, on Aug. 25, 2025. (AP Photo)

Moscow is largely spared from shortages
While officials appear to be concerned, the gasoline shortfall “isn’t system critical,” Peach said.

So far, the shortage remains confined to certain areas — the Far East and Crimea — because these regions usually are supplied by fewer refineries and present greater transportation demands.

Moscow has been spared the latest gasoline price spike because it is well-supplied from major refineries in Yaroslavl and Nizhny Novgorod, cities a few hours’ drive away. The capital also has a refinery in the city itself.

Russia is not at immediate risk of grinding to a halt — even in more vulnerable regions, experts say. Although private drivers may feel some pain at the gas pump, most buses and trucks run on diesel, for which Russia has a surplus. The military, which largely uses diesel fuel, also is insulated from any shocks.

Vakulenko wrote in a recent commentary that annual diesel production is “more than double than what is needed.”

That doesn’t mean the situation still couldn’t deteriorate. Refineries that make gasoline for Russia’s domestic market also make diesel and other products for export — a vital source of income amid heavy Western sanctions.

Industry observers say Ukraine’s drones target key refinery equipment, including the distillation column that separates incoming crude oil into other products, including gasoline, diesel, fuel for ships and asphalt. If damaged, it must be repaired or replaced for the refinery to function. Repairs could be difficult if foreign parts are needed.

The gasoline crisis is expected to ease by late September as demand subsides and the annual summer maintenance for many refineries is finished.

Still, the crisis highlights a vulnerability on the home front that has the potential to be exploited further as drone warfare evolves.

___

David McHugh in Frankfurt, Germany, and Joanna Kozlowska in London contributed to this report.

# why “go sooner” suddenly feels plausible
Ukraine’s refinery/energy hits + Crimea fuel couponing + IADS/radar attrition = classic **pre-culmination** pattern. In 2022 Kharkiv, shaping peaked, Russians culminated, then the hammer fell. ## RU culmination tells (fast check)
- **Fuel & fires:** sustained drop in daily artillery fires on one sector; visible **fuel rationing** to units.
- **AD rebalancing:** air-defense pulled off second-priority fronts to guard Kerch/land corridor.
- **Repair whack-a-mole:** rail/bridge fixes failing repeatedly within 24–72h.
- **Command noise:** sudden rotations, contradictory orders, milblogger panic spikes.
- **Civil strain in Crimea:** queues, couponing, staged “temporary relocations.”

If **3–4** of these light up on the same axis for a week, the window opens.

# the “Kursk-style” idea (breakthrough & hold ground of decision)
You don’t need a broad front. You need one **operational seam** where RU can’t sustain fires or fuel. Break through there, then **hold** over their LOCs while the logistics vise tightens behind you.

# what about **Rostov**?
Think of **Rostov-on-Don** less as a city to seize and more as a **node to switch off**:

- **Why it’s decisive:** Southern Military District HQ + **rail/highway confluence** feeding Donetsk/Luhansk, the Azov land corridor, and onward to Crimea. If Rostov’s bridges/rail yards/throughput are **functionally down**, the entire southeast starves faster—even if no ground crosses the border.
